speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Preliminary reports indicate a further decline in the economy in the third quarter of this year, which will make it the fifth consecutive quarter in which we have seen negative growth in the country. During that period some 540,000 Canadians have lost their jobs. The Minister indicated in his economic statement on October 27 that the turnaround in job creation would come in the fourth quarter. Given the continuing decline in the economy, does the Minister now stand by his forecast in October and, if so, does he expect to see some improvement in the unemployment figures which will be released this Friday?

Madam Speaker, in the statement 1 made to the House on October 27, I indicated at the time that indeed we expected there would be a continued decline in the third quarter and that we expected, however, there would be a turnaround in the fourth quarter. This is still our hope.

November 29, 1982
Oral Questions
As far as unemployment is concerned, I have indicated that it would remain very high and that it would decline only gradually during the course of next year. Thus I do not expect a decline in the rate of unemployment this Friday, but I do not have any more information in this regard than the hon. lady. We will await the reports of Statistics Canada in that regard.
That does not offer much hope either for those already unemployed or the ones who are fearing for their jobs today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same Minister. The GATT talks, as we all know, have failed to create the conditions for an expansion of world trade. Indeed, some countries may try to restrict their trade even further. That will make worse the opportunities for job creation here in Canada where 30 per cent of our economy is based on trade. Has this unsettling possibility been taken into consideration by the Minister and, if so, what effect will it have on his relatively optimistic forecast for 1983?

Madam Speaker, it is very unfortunate that the GATT ministers meeting did not come up with more productive results. Canada, which chaired the meeting in the person of the Minister of External Affairs, while there was also a delegation headed by the Minister of State for International Trade, did everything it could to strengthen the cause of anti-protectionism at this conference. Unfortunately, it seems we were not very successful. The Canadian Government is going to continue its campaign to encourage a lessening of the protectionist tendencies existing everywhere, including Canada. As far as our forecasts are concerned, these were made against the background that existed at the time, that is, in October 1982, and nothing that has happened since then, at the GATT conference, for instance, has provided any justification for changing them.

I guess there is a difference of opinion there, because what I am trying to indicate to the Minister is that things have worsened economically for Canada since he brought down his economic statement in October.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister will be meeting with his provincial counterparts on December 16, and given recent developments, the two that I have mentioned, that is, the continuing negative growth in the economy and the failure of the GATT talks, could he tell us what he plans to propose to provincial ministers in the way of new measures for job creation and growth in the country, or will he just sit back and let Canadians suffer
until the Macdonald Royal Commission brings in its interim report?

Madam Speaker, I have indicated that there would be only a gradual recovery, that we would see increases in the Gross National Product during the course of next year, and that the turnaround would come, we expected, during the last quarter of this year. I also indicated that, unfortunately, the rate of unemployment would decline very slowly.
I announced on October 27 a number of measures worth $1.1 billion. That amount comes on top of some $2.2 billion worth of various programs already announced by my predecessor. It takes a few weeks for programs to come into effect. The Minister of Employment and Immigration has consulted with his provincial colleagues already. Some provinces have not only supported our program but they have added funds to it, which is quite encouraging.
At the federal-provincial conference of Ministers of Finance we intend to review the economic situation together, to try to make sure our respective policies will reinforce each other rather than work at cross-purposes. We will be examining any steps that could be taken by the provincial Governments or the federal Government on the occasion of our respective budgets. I will have an opportunity to discuss the general thrust of my budget with my colleagues, and I expect that I will also be able to exchange views on how provincial ministers are preparing their own budgets which in most provinces, as the Hon. Member knows, come during the spring.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. It relates to the Youth of Canada. In 1968 when the present Grade 12 graduates were about four years old and the present university graduates were between seven and eight years of age, Canada had a balanced budget and a small national debt, yet we had the world's best health insurance, medicare and post-secondary education systems. Also we had a business climate that created jobs for all. We now find there are not enough jobs, the health insurance, medicare and post-secondary education systems are breaking down, the national debt is over $140 billion, and the yearly deficit is about $25 billion. Does the Prime Minister realize what his policies have done to young Canadians? They have denied them opportunities in a land which should be full of opportunities.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am happy to remind the Hon. Member that, during the entire course of the 1970s, Canada had the world record in job-creation of all industrial nations, and that is what our policies have done.

Madam Speaker, is the Prime Minister telling us that the whole Government existed just to create jobs in the
November 29, 1982

1970s? What about future planning for the children in the 1980s and the 1990s?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF YOUTH REPRESENTATIVE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, on the Macdonald Commission, for example, there is no member who could genuinely be said to represent youth. Why would the Prime Minister not have appointed some of the fine young business graduates, or university students, to sit on that Commission?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF YOUTH REPRESENTATIVE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am happy to see that the Hon. Member is lending his support to the Government's establishment of a Royal Commission to look at the 1980s and 1990s. If the Hon. Member is making representation for additional Commissioners, I am sure the Chairman of the Commission would be happy to receive that from him directly.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration, but in his absence I will direct it to the Minister of Finance. As the Minister knows, the NEED Program announced by him will employ only one in twenty of the unemployment insurance exhaustees this winter. The Minister of Employment and Immigration's study indicates that over 82 per cent of exhaustees are unable to find work in the first two months after their UI benefits run out. Surely the Minister knows that, in terms of human suffering, there will be an average of 10,000 more individuals every month in 1983 becoming UI exhaustees. What further plans does the Minister of Finance have for work or further financial assistance for these people?

Madam Speaker, I wish that my hon. friend would get his figures in line with those of other members of his Party who have said we will be helping only one in ten of the exhaustees under the NEED Program. Whatever the figure, it is quite clear that we will not be able to answer the unemployment problem that we are facing at the present time through that particular job-creation program.
As I have indicated before, there are a number of other programs that have been set up by the Government, particularly under the Minister of Employment and Immigration. We
Oral Questions
had put well over a billion dollars into direct job creation before the announcement of the NEED program and the $500 million I have mentioned.
We have also indicated that what is required for real and long lasting job creation is a lowering of the inflation rate and a lowering of the interest rates so that the private sector can get going again to create the jobs in the plants, firms, factories and various industries of the country. This is what we are working toward, trying to make sure that we will have recovery where the private sector will be the answer to growth again.

The Minister's soft talk sounds very nice in here, but for the people demonstrating today outside in the freezing rain, and the hundreds of thousands across the country who will be forced onto welfare this winter, it is of no comfort whatsoever.

Madam Speaker, the Minister refers to economic recovery. All knowledgeable indicators are stating at this time that there will not be a recovery and unemployment will not drop significantly for at least a year and possibly two years. In view of this fact I would ask the Minister, since the Government is also facing the prospect of seeing its welfare costs go up substantially this winter as Canadians are left with no other resort, will he instead extend unemployment insurance benefits for the first 26 weeks of 1983 for those Canadians who have exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits already and who are still unable to find work?

No, Madam Speaker. I might add, in answer to the Hon. Member, that in this particular regard we have already increased the premiums that are being paid by the workers and employers by some 40 per cent in order to meet the needs of those who are unemployed at the present time, and that the Government is assuming approximately 50 per cent of the total deficit in the fund at the present time. I am afraid that I cannot entertain the suggestion put forward by the Hon. Member in the current circumstances. I do not think that we can afford it.

I hope that the Minister fully appreciates the meaning of his answer. It means a greatly expanded burden on municipalities and provinces across the entire country, for welfare costs. Second, his few short words in that answer mean that literally tens of thousands of hard working Canadians will be forced onto welfare this winter. That is an absolute disgrace, and we in this Party are outraged.

How does the Minister justify asking Canadians, including all those unemployed Canadians out there looking for work, to accept the poverty of welfare as a way of life, because that is what he is asking?

November 29, 1982
Oral Questions
How does he justify that to those who are ready, able and willing to work, but cannot find it? How does he justify forcing them on welfare and saying, "I am sorry, that is the bottom line"?

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member's suggestion is just to extend more handouts. I am trying to tell him that, together, we should all try to build a situation where the private sector will again be able to hire people and get the economy growing again. That is what is very important and what we should all be pushing for together.
I indicated before, in my statement on October 27, that indeed, unemployment would remain very high, distressingly high. I share all those concerns of the Hon. Member. I am sure those concerns about the present situation are shared by many Canadians. However, there is no point in playing make-believe with the Canadian people on such a very important issue.

subtopic: ALLEGATIONS MADE IN BRITISH SPY TRIAL
ALLEGATIONS MADE IN BRITISH SPY TRIAL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General. This morning, at the Old Bailey in England, Hugh Hambleton went on trial under the Official Secrets Act on charges of spying. The Attorney General of Great Britain made certain allegations based on a statement made by Mr. Hambleton. Certain of those were as follows: first, that he had been a Soviet agent for more than 30 years, second, that he had contact with Soviet agents both in Paris and Quebec and that seven years ago he met Yuri Andropov, had dinner with him, and was encouraged to run as a candidate to become a Member of Parliament. Are those facts correct? Were they within the knowledge of the RCMP? Why was he prosecuted in Great Britain and not in Canada?
[DOT] (M30)

subtopic: ALLEGATIONS MADE IN BRITISH SPY TRIAL
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have not seen those statements that were reported by the Hon. Member, and I would like to wait until I do before commenting on them. I have said, and I will repeat, that the RCMP have co-operated with the British officials to bring this case to the point at which it is now, and that until the case is disposed of 1 should not say anything further about it.

maintopic: ROLE OF ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
ROLE OF ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext: I would like to ask the Solicitor General a brief supplementary question. Were the RCMP informed of all the information that I have alleged today? Is the Solicitor General aware of the facts pertaining to this individual, and did he have any discussions whatsoever with the RCMP on why the prosecution is taking place in Great Britain and not in Canada, notwithstanding the cooperation of the RCMP?

maintopic: ROLE OF ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext: I have indicated that the Department of Justice, through the Attorney General of Canada, advised that a prosecution founded in Canada, on the basis of the evidence that was available at a certain point, would not have been successful. Following that, the RCMP had other discussions with Mr. Hambleton himself, Mr. Hambleton departed for Great Britain, the RCMP had information obtained before and after the decision made by the Attorney General of Canada, and there was co-operation between the two friendly security agencies which have brought the matter to the point at which it is today. I think all of us should be pleased to see that justice is being done in the matter.

subtopic: RETURN OF CONVICTED MURDERER TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
RETURN OF CONVICTED MURDERER TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is also addressed to the Solicitor General. Over the weekend we were informed that Clifford Robert Olson is once again in British Columbia, ostensibly to give information and provide evidence related to certain unsolved murders in that Province. Can the Solicitor General give the House an ironclad guarantee that, in this instance, there are no further deals contemplated with Mr. Olson, either monetary or of another nature, and, in particular, can he give us the assurance the Mr. Olson has not been promised a transfer to Abbotsford or another British Columbia facility, that he has not been offered immunity from further prosecution and, finally, that he has not been offered any cash benefit for giving evidence? I wonder if the Solicitor General can direct himself to those questions.

subtopic: RETURN OF CONVICTED MURDERER TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: 1 can certainly confirm that Clifford Olson was taken by the RCMP to British Columbia last week under a court order obtained by the Government of British Columbia, by the Attorney General, from the Chief Justice of British Columbia, that Clifford Olson is there, that the investigation is under way, and that during the course of the investigation, which is totally under the direction of the Attorney General of British Columbia, I will not have anything to say about it.

maintopic: RECOVERY OF MONEYS PAID TO CONVICTED MURDERER
RECOVERY OF MONEYS PAID TO CONVICTED MURDERER
speechtext:
The Attorney General of British Columbia, just prior to the time the House resumed its session here, denied that it was his direction with respect to the transfer of Mr. Olson to British Columbia.
The Solicitor General's dealing with the Olson matter has been typified by confusion and obfuscation. Olson. maintopic: RECOVERY OF MONEYS PAID TO CONVICTED MURDERER

As to offenders profiting from their crimes, I have indeed been concerned about it. I have expressed my concern in correspondence sent to my provincial counterparts. There is currently a meeting of deputy ministers of law enforcement under way. It is one of the matters on their agenda.
I have put forward two or three suggestions on courses which might be taken to comply with that very fundamental concept of justice that an offender should not be able to benefit from his crime. However, as I indicated, and as my colleague, the Minister of Justice, has indicated in the House, it is a difficult matter. There is presently no legal machinery in place for depriving an offender of the profit from his crime. If a method were to be found, it would require legislation in this House, or legislation in one of the provincial legislatures, as I indicated in the letter that I sent to my counterparts. Therefore, the matter is under our consideration, but I do not have an answer for the Hon. Member yet.

REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CO-OPERATION ON ISSUE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Solicitor General. On May 4, 1982, he did indeed send a letter to the solicitor representing eight families involved in the Olson tragedy, in which he set out some of the constitutional and jurisdictional difficulties in prohibiting a murderer from profiting from publishing details of his murders. The Solicitor General has perhaps already answered in part the question I would have put to him. The letter, dated May 4, states on the third page:
I undertake to be available to meet with my provincial colleagues to see what uniform action may be taken.
He said, "circumstances do demand action". I would really like to ask the Solicitor General when the meeting with his provincial counterparts will take place. Is there any provincial Attorney General who objects to the appropriate amendment on the provincial scene, involving property and civil rights, which could dovetail with an amendment to the Criminal Code on the federal level, to ensure that those who commit murder are not able to profit from such murder? At the moment I am restricting it to murder.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CO-OPERATION ON ISSUE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, subsequent to the letter, I indicated some of the difficulties involved in a measure which could be seen by the courts as impinging on free speech, or expropriating property without compensation. These are two matters which are the subject of protections in the Charter or Rights and Freedoms and in basic principles of natural justice in our country.
Oral Questions
On the other hand, the goal is also one which is very much a matter of public policy, of wanting to prevent criminals from profiting from their crimes. I have received feedback from some of my provincial counterparts who have expressed concern in terms of the considerations that I have just mentioned. However, the meeting of deputies is taking place this week. The meeting of Ministers may take place in the early or late spring. That has not been settled and may depend, indeed, on the amount of progress which is made on these issues by the meeting of our deputies which begins tomorrow.

Madam Speaker, this matter has been kicking around for too many months. In view of the resurrection of the matter in the front pages of this land concerning the dirty deeds Mr. Olson committed, surely this is a lethargic approach to something which is a basic injustice. Not only to protect the civil right of the murderer, but also the collective right of the community and/or the sensitivity and anxiety of the parents involved, something must be done.
Could the Minister at least assure the House that, in terms of his jurisdiction now, and in terms of parole, there will be some type of restriction in a parole order prohibiting a murderer from directly publishing so that he can benefit? If these officials are to take so long, could he not give some instructions to the Law Reform Commission-God forbid-to come in with an objective assessment of the rights and wrongs, pros and cons, of this constitutional issue?
Surely the Minister must know that there are 28 States in the United States which already have legislation taking care of some of the concerns of the Minister, and that the interpretation of the Constitution in the United States is that there is no such thing as absolute freedom of speech when it involves sordid matters or murderers profiting from their murders.
Madam Speaker, I think that American jurisprudence is indeed helpful, but some of those States have found the measures that they put forward struck down as being invalid-
There hasn't been a murderer yet.

-under American law. Of course, Canadian law is different. My great worry is that we would see some method which would either be defeated in the court or some method which would work very well for the first case before us, but one which would create considerable difficulty down the road in cases which are not as easy and as obvious as the case involving Clifford Robert Olson.
Or the FLQ.

It is easy enough to know how to handle such a case, but what would be the consequences down the road of putting a measure in place which would perhaps result in other

November 29, 1982

Let's put something in place.

He said: Madam Speaker, it is with great pleasure and even greater satisfaction that I may present a motion in the House today which paves the way for parliamentary reform, a concept I have always cherished and a goal I have always wanted to achieve. Hon. members will remember and I am particularly reminded of this today the disappointment I felt in 1974 and 1975, during the first two years when I was sitting on the far southwest side of this House, and every time I wanted to take the floor, I sent a note to the Hon. James Jerome, the Speaker at the time, in order to be recognized. On occasion, I took part in debates which were equally disappointing to the vast majority of my colleagues on both sides of the House. The result was that from the very outset, I showed an interest in making a modest contribution by participating in the search for solutions that would help this institution to evolve and to be more in tune with reality. I also remember that in 1976, in our caucus on the government side, I was given responsibility for preparing a draft proposal on parliamentary reform. After consulting with a multitude of sub-committees specialized in various fields, we succeeded in drafting a proposal which, I may point out, is in many ways similar to the suggestions that were made today by the Special Committee on Parliamentary Reform and are embodied in the motion I have the honour of presenting.
Again, in 1976, in addition to taking part in the search for ways to make Parliament evolve, within the party caucus of Government members, I also remember spending several weeks during the summer, with a number of colleagues on both sides of the House, on the Committee on Procedure and Organization, a committee that managed to produce three reports which, unfortunately, were never presented to the

November 29, 1982
Parliamentary Reform
House, but, I am sure, were used just the same and which have most certainly influenced members who not long ago were working on the report that is before the House today. Subsequently, after my initial disenchantment and after my involvement in a reform proposal at the caucus level and as member of a standing committee of the House, I wanted to remain involved in the workings of Parliament. In fact, fate was on my side, because the responsibilities I have been given since 1977 have always kept me very close to parliamentary procedure, either as Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the House in 1977 and in 1978, or as Deputy Leader of the Official Opposition in the House in 1979, and, for two and a half years now, since March 1980, as Leader of the Government in the House and President of the Privy Council. Once again, this opportunity to present a motion that will mean a giant step towards parliamentary change is not only a great pleasure for me it also as I said at the beginning of my speech has a very special meaning for me.
I am also very pleased that this fundamental proposal should come at a time when this session has already seen such major historic measures as constitutional reform and our National Energy Policy. A session, which, as Hon. Members are aware, has broken all previous records by being the longest session ever and also because of the number and significance of the measures that have been adopted. Mr. Speaker, we first had to adopt a motion that would enable the Government to patriate the Constitution and adopt a Charter of Rights, we had to approve the many bills constituting the National Energy Program, we had to approve three budgets, the Estimates for four fiscal years and some 140 pieces of legislation and we had to debate many motions on subjects selected both by the Opposition and by individual Members. In other words, this House has had to wait since April 1980, the beginning of the current session, until finally agreement was reached on a reform proposal that is certainly beneficial, considering the manner in which Parliament achieved this result.
Before I go any further, I would first like to pay special tribute to someone whose receptiveness to all aspects of parliamentary change, has, since 1968, made it possible for this institution and its Members to evolve, and I am, of course, referring to the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau). The House will recall that it was under the present Prime Minister that in 1968, Parliament unanimously adopted, and it was unanimous, contrary to popular belief, since there was agreement between Members on both sides of the House, unanimously adopted on December 20, 1968, a major reform in the area of supply proceedings. Still under the present Prime Minister of Canada, television made its entrance in the House of Commons, thus bringing Parliament closer to the Canadian people, and again, under the present Prime Minister of Canada, first in 1975 and latterly in 1981, salaries and pensions of parliamentarians were adjusted to decent levels, and still under the present Prime Minister of Canada, we now have
the culmination of the developments of the past fourteen years, namely, this major step towards parliamentary reform, and it is the present Prime Minister who made this reform possible.
It was also under the Prime Minister that, besides all the reforms and changes I have talked about, funds have been provided for the caucus research bureaux, for the offices of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent), and for such funds not only to be increased but in some circumstances even to be created. That is most important when we talk in terms of re-evaluating the role of the Member of Parliament in whichever side of the House he or she sits.
The House will recall that in 1968 no funds were provided for caucus research bureaux. It was in the fall of 1968 that the Government announced its intention to provide such funds, beginning in the 1969-70 fiscal year. In 1969-70 the amount provided for the Official Opposition was $125,000, and for each of the smaller Opposition Parties-because there was more than one at that time-$35,000. These amounts were originally paid through the Leader's office.
Starting in 1970 the caucus research bureaux were created as separate entities and a Liberal caucus research bureau was added. For 1982-83 the caucus research bureaux received the following amounts-and this is where we see the changes: Liberals, $601,000; Progressive Conservatives, $541,000; and NDP, $285,000.
The Office of the Leader of the Opposition did not have a separate budget until 1980, under the Prime Minister. In 1968-69 the figure for the Office of the Leader of the Opposition was about $87,500; in 1969-70 the Leader of the Opposition received $129,500 and the Leader of the New Democratic Party received $36,000. In 1982-83, under the Prime Minister, the Office of the Leader of the Opposition had a budget of $1,081,400 and the Office of the Leader of the NDP $569,700, both amounts separate from the funds of the research bureaux of the caucuses.
That is a reality that we do not talk about very often, but it is a reality that makes it possible for Members on both sides to come here and deliver better speeches and do a better job as Members of Parliament; or, at least, it should allow them to do a better job as representatives of their constituents.
The point I want to make in saying "thank you" to the Prime Minister is that since 1968 many changes have been made in this place, some of which are more obvious than others, but all of which were most important. They start with the reform by unanimous consent in 1968 of the Business of Supply, going through to this very substantial increase in research bureau funds of each caucus, to the funds allocated for the offices of the Leaders of both Opposition Parties, to broadcasting the debates of this House in 1978, to the increases in our salaries and pensions and to the reform we are discussing today.

I would also like, Mr. Speaker, to pay a special tribute to the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure, especially its Chairman, the Hon. Member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre), and each of the members of the Committee for having come to a unanimous agreement on changes which, as I noted earlier, match almost exactly those I have always advocated and through which Parliament will better reflect the reality of the eighties. Finally, I want to pay homage to all those, men and women, who have contributed directly or indirectly to this result.

The process of reform of parliamentary procedure is, by the very nature of the institution, an ongoing one. In Canada the first major reforms came only at the turn of the century. It was almost 50 years later that the next major revisions took place. Then in the 1960s a series of committees and experiments, of which our present efforts are a part, began. Since the major revisions of 1968-69 we have had many committee investigations on the matter. We have tried several experiments and have even adopted some permanent changes. Once again, we have before us some proposed experiments and it is interesting to note that one of the proposals is for an automatically continuing committee review of our rules.
The Special Committee, of course, benefited from superprofessional assistance from the committee's branch and the table research office and was particularly assisted by the former Clerk of the House, Mr. Alistair Fraser, whose wisdom, experience and subtlety of mind permeates the report.
My predecessor as Government House Leader, Leaders on both sides of the House, and our staffs, some of whom are still with us, some of whom have gone to greener pastures, all contributed in one way or another to this report. Although he was unable to participate in this committee, the report most certainly reflects years of work by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
Finally, although I never had the privilege of meeting the reputed grand master of parliamentary procedure as former Clerk Assistant of the House, one who knew him well told me: "If Gordon Dubroy was alive today, this is exactly what he would have produced".

The proposed experiment, Mr. Speaker, is interesting and relevant for three reasons. First, it will help to upgrade the role played by Members of Parliament. It will make Parliament more alive and more effective, without eroding the right of the opposition to a full debate. Finally, the third reason why this experiment will be interesting is that it will update Parliament and give it more respectability in the eyes of the Canadian people. To summarize, the role of Members of Parliament will be upgraded, Parliament will become more alive and more effective without infringing upon the rights of the opposition to
Parliamentary Reform
a full debate. Parliament will be a more modern institution, more respectable, and more respected by the people, at least I hope so. If we go through the nine proposed changes, we can see that they will have these three results. I believe that every one of the proposed changes will have this effect. Of course, this is more obvious in the case of some changes, but even with the others, we shall have partly achieved these results.
The first proposed change concerns the parliamentary calendar which we wanted to implement for a long time and which our predecessors had already considered when looking at possible reforms. This calendar will finally allow Members of Parliament to plan ahead realistically and will make it possible for the Government to announce in good faith and on a regular basis,-at least three times during a session or at the beginning of each semester,-to Parliament and the opposition its legislative program the weeks and months to come. Of course, this program will not be restrictive and the Government will always be able to add to it, but if we want to benefit from the experience there must be no abuse of changes and 1 believe the Government is quite willing to make public regularly at the beginning of each semester its proposed legislative program to the Canadian Parliament. At the same time, the opposition will be in a better position to coordinate its strategy against whatever legislation it finds more controversial.
We can see immediately that a parliamentary calendar with three semesters and adjournments at set dates will promote efficient planning both for the Government and the Members of the opposition, and I am convinced that it will make Parliament even more productive, not because the opposition will be more prepared not to debate Government legislation, but rather because it will be able to make a preliminary choice of the subjects it finds most interesting and to use the time allocated to discuss Government proposals and allow passage of less controversial bills, which unfortunately was not always the case under the present system. As concerns this first change, I would also emphasize that the parliamentary calendar will not decrease the workload of Members of Parliament. It will not reduce their hours of work. On the contrary as a result of the changes implemented today we shall sit an average of 175 days a year, while the previous average was 165 days. We shall therefore have a heavier workload and ten more sitting days, and the proposed changes do not limit in any way the daily sitting hours of Parliament from Monday to Friday inclusively.
It is clear, therefore, that this parliamentary calendar will contribute significantly to upgrade the role of Members of Parliament. It should be conducive to better planning, greatly reduce or eliminate many of the frustrations many of us feel- I think that, in that area, the benefits will be obvious-and make Parliament more effective and, therefore, more streamlined and better perceived by the Canadian people.
As to the day sittings, the committee recommended that instead of sitting for two hours in the evening on Monday,

November 29, 1982
Parliamentary Reform
Tuesday and Thursday, the Elouse should sit between 11 a.m. and 1 p.m. Again, this is an extremely positive change, which I have always supported, not only because it will make life easier for Members of the House, although there is nothing wrong in trying to improve the life style of parliamentarians, many of whom are men and women with family responsibilities, but also because it will make it possible for them to work harder in the afternoon than they can now in the evening when they are tired and, consequently, the tone of the debate suffers. Hon. Members will be more available in the evening for committee sittings, which will be more interesting. The smaller committees will sit more often because they will be busier, for reasons I will indicate in a little while. The parties on both sides of the House will also be able to hold special caucuses in the evening without any risk of coming into conflict with House sittings. And finally, Hon. Members on both sides of the House will be able to work quietly in the evening without fear of being interrupted by bells ringing in every hallway of Parliament, of having to cancel public engagements they might have both in Ottawa or in communities located within a reasonable distance from the capital, where they would be addressing the Canadian people, as they are duty bound to do.
The fact that Members of Parliament would not have to sit in the evening will upgrade their role in the sense that they would not have to answer slavishly to the call of the bell until 10:30 p.m. three nights a week, but that after 6:00 p.m., they would be free to come and go as they please, to look after the interests of their constituents, to sit on the standing committees of the House, to participate actively in the special caucuses of their respecting parties, to go and address the Canadian people in many communities located within a reasonable distance from Ottawa. This is an aspect which I feel is extremely positive and which will have a major impact on the way Hon. Members will perform in the House and assume their responsibilities in a more humane and, consequently, more involved, interesting and effective fashion.
The suggestion to limit speeches to 20 minutes, followed by a debate lasting some ten minutes, 1 find most original. I do not know how the debate will progress. This is a chance which I feel we are taking, and that we are all a little curious and worried about the way this experience will unfold, but as we are people of good will, we all want this experience to succeed, and I am sure that this type of original suggestion will achieve its purpose. Firstly, if speeches are shortened, they will be more interesting and to the point, and secondly, our debates will be livelier. As I was reading part of my remarks a moment ago, some of my colleagues opposite could not help commenting on it, and I realized that I was becoming boring; I quickly moved on to the subject matter of my speech, but as my notes were in English, I wanted to be sure to congratulate all those who deserved it.
But I think that after mid-January the 20-minute speeches will preclude long quotations, make the debates more lively
and certainly more relevant since any Member rising to speak may have to answer questions and prove in no uncertain terms that he knows what he is talking about. And then, of course, speeches at the report stage will be cut down to ten minutes; that will speed up the debate and do away with tedious repetitions. The report stage of a bill will be more constructive and we will be able to proceed with third reading much more rapidly.
Another change which will enhance the role of Hon. Members, and make Parliament more interesting and definitely more modern is the fact that votes to be taken on Fridays will be deferred. Considered on its own, such a change is not particularly challenging, but taken in conjunction with others like shorter speeches, the new parliamentary schedule and the proposed over-all reform, I suggest that Hon. Members will be less in a partisan mood on Fridays because, any vote on a substantive matter being deferred, they will probably be more inclined to dispose quickly of the so-called non-controversial bills. It will be possible to clear the Order Paper of the many bills which are often absolutely essential, of a technical nature, or urgent for other reasons. We will be able to pass such bills without the fear of having to call Hon. Members for a vote since any recorded division will be automatically deferred until the following Monday. As a result, Hon. Members will be happier and healthier as well in the planning of their weekend activities in their riding or elsewhere in Canada. They will be having a few extra hours to travel and meet with their constituents in their respective ridings, feeling a lot more alert and less tired by last minute travelling crowded within two days as is the case now.
We are doing away with that parliamentary oddity, Standing Order 43, a move which practically all Hon. Members fully endorse. It is a proceeding which no longer serves any useful purpose, although there still will be a way to move an urgent motion in an institution such as ours. I would suggest however that if a motion is indeed really urgent and important, as Hon. Members are now required to explain in their preliminary remarks under Standing Order 43, I should think that if something very important and very urgent does come up, unanimous consent will be forthcoming without any recourse to a special rule. We will have the usual discussions between House leaders and/or the interested parties with a view to adopting any really important and urgent motion without debate and undue haste. Doing away with motions under Standing Order 43 is in itself a very positive step. Instead, Hon. Members will each have 90 seconds to make a point rather than raise objections.
I think we should try it on an experimental basis because I am convinced that those who want that experiment to succeed will draw maximum benefits from those 15-odd minutes before the Question Period and not make ill use of the time of the
November 29, 1982

House. I hope that the Chair, mindful of the intent of the committee report, will recognize Hon. Members without any regard for party affiliation and that the time available will be equally distributed between both sides of the House.
With respect to Wednesday afternoon being devoted to Private Members' Business, as in many other instances we would have favoured other alternatives such as Monday morning from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., or Friday, but we on the Government side have agreed to that change as we did to others so that the experiment could be carried out. Since Private Members' Business will be dealt with on the same day,
I hope that Hon. Members who want to introduce bills or move motions will find it easier to better organize their work and plan those measures for a specific day of the week. This might deprive the Government of the choice of one day in allotting opposition days. However, I am convinced that on a special occasion, as more experience is gained, if either the Government or the Opposition wish to earmark a particular Wednesday as an allotted day, this could be done by unanimous consent by agreeing to have Private Members' Business postponed to another day.
Another positive change is the one respecting quorum. Too often, the image of Members of Parliament has been tarnished by someone trying to make political gains out of an unfortunate circumstance whereby some Members happened not to be in their seats, thus preventing quorum. I believe that every time a count was called for lack of quorum, this was a disservice to this institution, to the parties in this House and certainly to Members of Parliament in general. Nobody is to be blamed really, because very often this happened during fierce debate when it was too tempting to avail oneself of the Rules. Those who objected seized this opportunity to express their disapproval and call the public's attention by having Parliament adjourn, because Hon. Members were meeting in committee or phoning in the Government anteroom, or attending to their business and functions. I believe that this temptation will disappear when the suggested change is implemented because whenever fewer than 20 Members are present in this House and an Hon. member calls attention to this and the Speaker is aware of this fact, the House will not be called for a count until the bells have rung for 15 minutes. And in such cases Hon. Members meeting in committees or attending to other Parliament Business will certainly hurry back to their seats in order that the House and committees may work simultaneously.
The other changes also are very important. They deal with the structure of our Standing Committees. Suggestions are made as to Special Committees and the reduction of committee membership in my view will have a most important impact. I, for one, have always supported that change, because it is my belief that a small group can much better and more easily concentrate on an important matter, as evidenced by the Special Committees that were established last year and made reports on matters of current interest. My parliamentary
Parliamentary Reform
secretary had the privilege to chair one of those on the handicapped. They did tremendous work. They were seven. They drew their report within a reasonable time frame. The same may be said for the Chairman of the Committee on Parliamentary Reform, the Hon. Member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre). Experience has shown that smaller and more flexible committees, when entrusted with interesting matters, can have a very positive impact on the development of our parliamentary system, upgrade the role of Members of Parliament, sharpen their interest and ultimately enable this institution to produce much more enlightened measures that better meet the wishes of the Canadian people.
Therefore smaller committees, with 10 to 15 members, would be busier because all reports tabled before Parliament under a statute would automatically be referred to those committees. They would always have bills before them and estimates, as well as those reports tabled before Parliament that do not require special reference. In each of these committees, therefore, about ten members will be able to examine topics they are most interested in and submit reports to this House, to which the Government will have to respond intelligently in a limited time frame and which could afterwards be made public in due time. Finally, this ongoing review of regulations by the Committee on Procedure and Organization also seems to me like a constructive suggestion. 1 believe that this experience should be evaluated as it proceeds so that we may make adjustments if need be, not to undermine the experiment or long-term parliamentary reform, but rather to make this experimental process easier with a view to bringing about a more efficient, human and modern Parliament.
I would have liked to mention an area which those who deal with parliamentary reform will have to examine during the next few months, namely supply procedure, budget confidentiality, budgetary bills, financial bills and the delays involved as a result of our outmoded procedure which forces us years after a budget has been brought down, to still have to debate bills ensuing from past budgets. I believe this kind of reform now deserves special consideration and a consensus will not be easily reached when it comes to firm conclusions. Not only will such a reform be a challenge, but 1 believe that is most relevant and that if Parliament is to be in a better position to deal with today's problems, our procedure dealing with supply, the budget and supply bills will have to be updated so that the House of Commons can deal with these matters within a reasonable time. I believe that one of the ways to dispose of bills more quickly and to avoid many delays would be to allow preliminary consultation of all the people concerned before a budget is made public and related bills are tabled.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to invite all Members of Parliament to make this experiment a success and not to look for anomalies or weaknesses in this proposal, since it is

November 29, 1982
Parliamentary Reform
not perfect as we recognize ourselves and as I think our friends opposite and the members of the Committee also recognize. The rules proposed to this House have weaknesses and unclear elements, and I believe that for a destructive mind, it would be very easy although childlish to prevent this experiment from being positive and successful. I therefore call on the intellectual honesty of all Members and I want to assure them of the sincerity of the Government in implementing the proposed changes so that this experiment can be a success and result in fact in permanent changes to which adjustments may be made. Therefore parliamentarians on both sides of the House will feel more useful in society, will feel truly upgraded and, convinced that it is to their advantage to work in committees and that they can make a difference on legislation introduced in this House. As I said, it would be easy enough to botch the exercise, but to me it would be totally unacceptable and irresponsible. I think that it is merely a matter of credibility, not for the Government, not for the Official Opposition, not for Hon. Members collectively, not for the independent Member, it is a matter of credibility for each and everyone of us. It is a matter of credibility for this institution itself and it is essential as we are experiencing special problems confronting our community and while our economic and social development requires major changes during the years to come. It is essential for a democratic institution such as our Parliament to be in a position to respond to reality and adjust to our modern times, to the eighties. I think that the proposed reform is not the only solution but it is a step in the right direction. At long last, this institution will be operating within the framework of a series of Standing Orders which given the good faith and the practical sense of its Members will ensure a performance that will be more readily accepted by Canadians and will meet their aspirations.
Finally, 1 hope that this experience and the permanent changes to be implemented at a later date will pave the way to a regular and continued development. I regret that we should introduce by fits and starts such revolutionary reforms which contrast too strongly with the bad habits acquired by Parliament. I think that the suggestion that we let the Committee on Procedure and Organization constantly monitor the implementation of our Standing Orders will from now on allow parliamentary reform to proceed on a daily basis, and develop at a more regular pace without suddenly having every 12 , 14 or 15 years to make recommendations which following some experimentation become a step in the right direction. In conclusion I wish we will all show good faith, goodwill, and a practical mind so that parliamentary reform will become a continued procedure in the process of a normal and regular development to allow once again elected representatives to work proudly in the best interests of their constituents so that our democratic institution may play its true role and increasingly gain the respect of all Canadians.

We are all happy to see that many of his suggestions contained in that discussion paper have now seen the light of day in the changes which have been proposed by the Special Committee.
The House Leader has described the third report as a giant step forward. Reform, as a whole, would certainly constitute a giant step forward. The references of the House Leader to the moneys which have been made available to the Opposition Parties and to the Office of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) bear one brief reflection. I see the Government House Leader shaking his head in the

negative, but I believe if he checks he will find that to be accurate. Changes to our Standing Orders and to our practices have a habit of being unable to foresee situations arising in the future, the effect of which is never anticipated by ourselves in a debate such as this or by committee members who bring forward the recommendations.
I might also say that, as I develop my remarks in this discussion, it is my intention to set forth certain understandings upon which we are accepting this third report on an experimental basis and to say, quite frankly, that within that one-year period we expect those understandings to be fulfilled in good faith and in the good spirit intended by the committee in the report. Parliamentary Reform
sense it was the former Clerk of this Elouse who contributed to my presence here today, and that, he made that contribution in 1957 during the first election in which I ran. You might ask him, in a private moment, to explain that to you, Mr. Speaker.
I want to deal with the report generally. It is our feeling that Parliament maintains its power, integrity and prestige by remaining at arm's length from the bureaucracy and the Government. Parliament cannot allow itself to become a pensioner of the Government no matter how benevolent or how well-intentioned. Parliament cannot afford to become the private personal property of whatever Government might find itself in office from time to time.
Parliament is the highest resort of freedom, where free men and women are able to voice opinions and to criticize the excesses of powerful Governments without fear of retaliation. Parliament's independence, if that is to be the case, must be the primary concern of every citizen.
If Parliament is to carry out its mandate of controlling expenditures and overseeing the activities of Government so that the resources of the taxpayers do not become simply an instrument for retaining Governments in power, then Parliament must be free of coercion, intimidation or restraint. Parliament no longer needs to fear the pressure from an allpowerful royal court. Just as inimical to free deliberation is the pressure from a Government which would like to become allpowerful. I say these things without any intention whatsoever of being partisan.
Proposals for parliamentary reform usually aim at gaining more time for Government business and reducing the time available to an Opposition. From my personal viewpoint, the proposals of this committee fall into that latter category because there is no doubt in my mind that the changes contained in this third report are overwhelmingly in favour of the Government.
We, nonetheless, are prepared, on an experimental basis, to adopt the third report in the hope-and we have this sincere hope-that the Government will act bona fide and in good faith in the manner in which it used the excess advantages which they will gain as a result of these changes, and in the singular anticipation that we are going to see further changes in subsequent reports that will result in that kind of fiscal and over-all parliamentary control of Government and the purse strings. Those reports have yet to come.
Let me point out at once that what diminishes the Opposition diminishes Parliament and Parliament's ability to act. It is very clear that if there is to be effective criticism on a continuing basis it will come from the Opposition. Parliament is not strengthened, nor is the public interest served, by Members of Parliament who speak with emotion outside the House of Commons about the iniquity of certain legislation and yet who rise in the House of Commons and vote with the Government simply because they feel that that is their obligation, or that unless they do their careers will be deleteriously affected.
Parliament cannot afford-this is in keeping with those who hold the view that there are certain functions of this place for which there should be freedom to vote as a Member pleases- to have what have often been referred to as trained seals on either side of the House. That is why it is essential that the rights of the Opposition be preserved and that we maintain the capacity of the Opposition to make its position known in the most effective manner possible.
A simple numerical majority does not give a Government the right to ride like a juggernaut over the Opposition. Responsible Government also means taking minority views into account and paying attention to the position taken by the Opposition. Failing that, if we do not accept that principle as lying at the heart of our parliamentary system, we may as well accept, from my personal point of view, a one-party system such as that which now prevails in Poland under General Jaruzelski.
The last major reform undertaken in 1968 had the effect of removing much of the detail of both legislation and expenditure from the control of the House, relegating it to Government-dominated committees about which I will have more to say shortly. Obviously, this does not improve Parliament's capacity to deal with expenditure control.
In recent years we have had repeated warnings from successive Auditors General that Government expenditures are now completely removed from the control of Parliament. A vital brake on the excesses of Government since the days of Charles II has been control of expenditures by Parliament. To all intents and purposes, what those successive Auditors General are saying is that that brake no longer exists.
This is more than a mere question of procedure. It is a question of fundamental democracy, a question of the people's right to know how their money is being spent and to call the Government to account. That right has been lost. It has been lost totally, and that is not an exaggeration. It is one of the most important functions of this Special Committee, and that is one of the principal reasons that we accept on an experimental basis this report.
One of the most important functions of this committee is to regain that right and to regain, consequently, democracy in this country. Because unless this Special Committee comes up with a solution to the problem which has been pointed out by those successive Auditors General, and unless it can come up with that kind of solution which strikes at the heart of the reason for being of this place, then not only it but we will have failed.
I see some distinct encouragement that the committee is grappling with that problem from a very excellent paper which I have studied and which is now before the committee, I believe, under the combined authorship of the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) and the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mr. Lachance), who I see listening intently to this debate. It is a good thing to see a member on the Government
November 29, 1982

side and a member of the Opposition sponsoring, in a common cause, a proposed solution to the very important problem of which I speak. The first thing which must be restored in the procedures of this House is a mechanism whereby Parliament regains control over expenditures.
Coming now to the proposals themselves in the third report,
I re-emphasize my agreement with the words expressed by the subcommittee in the presentation of this report, that we should be looking at the proposals as a whole and not piecemeal. I reemphasize the importance of that and say that is precisely what we will be doing in the coming year. Because within that year I am sure, Mr. Speaker, we are going to see further reports dealing with very important problems, such as parliamentary control over expenditures. We will move cautiously in the meantime. We wait for the total reformation package before making these changes permanent, which should happen well within one year from today, and we may then consider the package as a whole. The dangers inherent in doing otherwise, 1 think, are so obvious they need not be set forth by me here today.
We are adopting this report now on the basis of an expectation of those reports yet to come which will deal meaningfully with the changes that are necessary. The Opposition, by this interim report, this third report, are being asked to give up a great many protections while the Government is giving up virtually nothing. As an example, the Opposition generally loses its power to delay or even block unacceptable legislation. In the meantime, the Government gains very substantially in terms of parliamentary time which the Opposition must surrender.
The adoption of the parliamentary calendar, while perhaps justifiable on a strictly experimental basis, and certainly justifiable for the convenience particularly of those Members who have families and long distances to travel, certainly adds something in the order of ten days, as stated by the Government House Leader; but I think it is more in the nature of in excess of three weeks' time which will be available to the Government. This would be tolerable if the Government showed some inclination to bring Bills forward in a proper and efficient manner, but we have seen nothing of that in the over 400 days we have been sitting in this session. After more than 400 days in the present session, we are faced with Ways and Means proposals arising out of three different budgets, some at cross-purposes with each other in a kind of confusion and chaos that no amount of rules changes or goodwill on the part of the Opposition can cure. Sitting on the Order Paper today are something like 46 or 47 Ways and Means motions, the product of three different budgets. This is simply bad management on the part of a Government which really does not know where it is at or where it is going in terms of its fiscal policies. The point I raise is that no procedural reform can make up for incoherence, lack of planning and lack of direction on the part of the Government.
Since this is the first opportunity I have had since last April to do so, I would like to refer to the episode of the energy omnibus Bill which was dumped into the lap of Parliament with the expectation by the Government that the House was
Parliamentary Reform
prepared to deal with a package which wrapped up something like 12 separate legislative enactments in one hydra-headed Bill. That is not the way I understand Parliament, and I believe that is a view shared by all in my Party.
I know that the Special Committee is grappling with this problem, and, indeed, it is a problem lo try to spell out criteria upon which omnibus Bills are designed or criteria which will prevent abuse of the device of omnibus Bills. We expect great things from the Special Committee when dealing with that subject matter, as we do when it deals with the subject of parliamentary control over expenditures. But no Government, no matter what pressures might be upon it to get their legislative programs through, is entitled to abuse Parliament to the extent where they confine us to divide once on a plethora of measures involving several principles upon which divisions could very well be different on all.
We are prepared to provide the Government with extra time through a parliamentary calendar if there can be some assurance that the Government will make use of that time in an appropriate way. We expect the Government to bring down a legislative program in keeping with the needs of Canadians, having regard to the very pressing economic, personal and human problems which are confronting Canadians in our country today. We expect to have the broad lines of that program in plenty of time to be able to deal effectively with it and for the opposition to make a positive contribution. So far we see no evidence that that is going to be done and, presumably, that also is going to be the subject of future reports of the committee.
There is a proposal to restrict votes on Friday. There are some concerns which 1 feel should be expressed with respect to that proposal. Nothing benefits a Government more and an Opposition less, given our existing practices and procedures, than predictability. One of the few weapons which an Opposition commands to prevent Government abuse of power is the lack of that predictability. One of the abuses which is open to them-and we are willing to run the risk to see if the good faith the Government House Leader speaks about will be displayed-is that the Government could schedule termination of controversial debates on a Friday knowing full well there would be no vote on a Friday and knowing also full well that that vote would be set over to a Monday. Therefore, if the good faith of which the Government House Leader spoke is not present in the experimental period, it could ensure that Fridays will become some kind of repository for ending controversial legislation, enabling the Government to put over votes on such legislation until the following Monday.
Another thought that occurred to me over the weekend is this. Supposing the summer session ended on a Friday and we were dealing with legislation requiring a vote. Given no unanimous consent, would that mean that all those votes would be put over until the fall when we came back? The possibility is there in the rules. I do not mention that for the purpose of nitpicking, but just to confirm what the Government House

November 29, 1982
Parliamentary Reform
Leader has said, that the proposals are far from perfect even as they stand now.
