speechtext: That is the problem.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
He acknowledges the problem. This is the kind of procedure which has inherent dangers which require a very careful look.
I do not know whether I heard the translation correctly when the Government House leader was winding up his remarks, but he referred to an experimental period for the adoption of the changes proposed in the third report, which would become permanent at the end of the year. I am sure I must have heard wrongly or that it came across wrongly. That happens to me often.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Why does my hon. colleague not speak French?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Well, I do not speak French all that well. I certainly know what the Minister is saying about me in the elevator, though!
In any event, we have to look at these changes very carefully. I really see no requirement for increasing to three hours the time required for giving notice under Standing Order 26. It is there and we are going to support it on an experimental basis, but I think its flaws will show themselves very quickly.
As for Standing Order 43, from my personal point of view there is no doubt of its usefulness in getting special attention drawn to special issues. I was rather surprised when I looked up the record a week ago to find that since the beginning of this session some 170 motions made under Standing Order 43 have been adopted. I could not believe that. I thought I had either miscounted or misconstrued, but looking through the Order Paper it is just fantastic the number that have gotten through. In any event, I agree that the procedure is rather useless and I do not think that the statements of a minute and a half are going to much lessen the farce. I would far rather like to see that 15-minute period used for extending Question Period. However, it is worth a try and we will see how it works. If it does not work I would suggest the committee go back to the drawing board and consider including that period as part of the Oral Question Period, making it a total of an hour.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in agreeing to shorter time limits on speeches the Opposition is giving up a considerable amount of time. Again, this could perhaps be more palatable or tolerable if we could expect the Government to bring forward a legislative program in some sort of planned way, but we see no evidence of this. By my calculations, and dealing only with the combined Opposition, the limitation on speech times has resulted in reducing the total available time in any debate from 4,080 minutes to 1,053 minutes, or a reduction at second reading stage of some 74.20 per cent. That is a considerable amount of available time to give up. At report stage we are giving up 50 per cent of the time and at third reading stage
some 25 per cent of the time. The Government gains all that time and in return there is precious little except for perhaps the most significant proposal by the Special Committee when it deals with the work of our standing committee system. But there is no significant giving up of anything to achieve that balance between Government and Opposition which is so essential.
So on average, sir, this one device of limiting speaking time results in transferring some 49 per cent of the Opposition's over-all time to the Government, and I do not believe that this can be described as an improvement in procedure. I can describe it as something with which we are prepared to go along because the issue parliamentary control over expenditures is so fundamental and important that we are prepared to go along initially with this report to see whether that is going to happen. If it does not happen, then that understanding upon which we are accepting this report will have failed and the experiment will, with great reluctance, have come to an end. So I am putting great store in that Huntington-Lachance paper on expenditure control, as we all are on this side of the House.
On the question of committees, I do not believe that our problem in the past has been too many members, although that always is subject to improvement. Perhaps we have too many committees, some 26 standing committees of the House of Commons now, and I think that once we solve the problem of Members, we will solve the problem of substitutions. Right now there are standing committees of the House which overlap, which cover the same territory, and there are committees which meet so infrequently that they constitute scarcely more than a nullity in our process. So this implies a need for tightening up the number of committees required to conduct the business of the House of Commons, and perhaps that is one of the matters the Special Committee will be looking at as well.
The proposal which the Government House Leader had so much praise for a moment ago, the automatic referral of annual reports, is one significant change which is beneficial. It is not just the annual reports which have automatic referral, but to use the words of the changes in the Standing Order, it includes all annual reports of Government Departments, Crown corporations, including their subsidiaries, and other agencies, which are to be referred to the appropriate standing committee. It also includes returns or other papers that are laid before the House in accordance with an Act of Parliament.
I see two very serious difficulties with that. Perhaps the most serious, and I think this may well have been overlooked by committee members, is that even given the very desirable change in the Standing Order, there is no mandatory provision for the committee to meet. If the Government does not wish the committee to meet, it will not meet. So that addresses itself again to the good faith that we are expecting the Government to exercise in causing these committees to meet immediately. As soon as the session opens, those standing committees should be struck and should be meeting. In the interim the Special
November 29, 1982

Committee should be considering, in one of its forthcoming reports, proposing an amendment to our Standing Orders which will make it obligatory for these committees to meet and not leave it to the whim of the Government. I do not suggest that such a thing would happen, but a Government could abuse that change. It might be embarrassing to let the standing committee, which might have, for instance, responsibility for looking into contracts in Banff National Park, meet at this particular time. That obligation should be there, but it is not there now.
The second omission that I see in the automatic referral is that time and time again, notwithstanding the existence of statutory law requiring annual reports to be tabled within a specific calendar time, those reports and papers have not been tabled and the returns have not been made. I have seen annual reports of Crown agencies that were supposed to be tabled within a fiscal year not tabled for two years. So much for automatic referral of annual reports if the law is disregarded in the first place. In that case, the committee has nothing to review.
The third weakness I see is that the requirement that the Government must respond to the report of the committee is only triggered if the Government majority on the committee requires the response. If you look carefully, Mr. Speaker, you will see that the response is at the request of the committee. The committee is going to continue to have a Government majority, and unless that majority agrees to require a response by the Government, that is not going to be forthcoming. I do not suggest for a moment that this would happen, but in the past I have known of committee chairmen from the Government side going to a Minister and saying that the committee has in mind to recommend such and such a thing, and would he find that embarrassing or would he accept it? I can see a Minister saying that the action would embarrass him considerably and asking the committee not to make him respond. That requirement is rather toothless, therefore.
I hope the Special Committee will address those concerns. If it is serious about improving the committee system, it will make meetings of committees obligatory.
I do not know how you can improve a law which requires annual reports to be tabled by a specific date. I hope the committee will address itself to that problem and to the question of the Government majority emasculating the requirement of Government response to committee reports.
With respect to special committees, I am quite puzzled by the proposal which would authorize a member of the committee or authorize the committee to make public interim and final reports, even though the House is not sitting. I find that rather surprising. What the House is authorizing, if the proposal is adopted, is that a special committee of the House could report to the media instead of to the House. If that is what the majority of Members want to try for a year, we will see how it works.
Parliamentary Reform
I want to return for a moment an aspect of to this automatic referral of annual reports that I did not pick up in my first remarks on the subject. On page 19 of the report, after the reference to Standing Order 41, there appears the following:
"(4) Reports, returns or other papers laid before the House in accordance with an Act of Parliament shall thereupon be deemed to have been permanently referred to the committee designated by the Member tabling the report, return
or paper."
We know that only Government members can table reports, returns or papers; Members of the Opposition cannot table anything. This is a substantive change which I am not sure committee members wanted to make. At present such reports, returns and papers may be tabled only by Ministers or their Parliamentary Secretaries. What we are doing here is authorizing any Government Member to table a report and refer it to any committee he or she pleases. Perhaps that was not the intention. Perhaps the reasoning was that a Minister or a Parliamentary Secretary is also a Member. I want to point out the procedural difficulty, however, if a Member who is not a Minister or a Parliamentary Secretary were to discharge that function, which he or she would be perfectly entitled to do as a result of that change.
I want to make sure that Members appreciate what they are doing, on the adoption of this report, with respect to Private Members' Business. Because this session has lasted as long as it has-the longest in our history at well over 400 days- Private Members' Bills have not been discussed since March 24, 1981. When it comes to dealing with Private Members' Business in the House, this is one area where I believe the Government or the Opposition has no right to interfere. Private Members have precious few legislative privileges. Private Members' hour has traditionally been the time in the whole process which is peculiarly the property of Private Members.
Since March 24, 1981 Private Members have been denied the right to debate Bills. All they have had is Thursdays and Fridays; in effect, what they have been denied is two hours per week. In the first Supply period of the three semester periods, 40 hours of Private Members' time has been denied since March 24, 1981. By the change proposed in the committee report, which we are prepared to try for an experimental year, Private Members lose one hour per week. Three hours on Wednesday is all they will get. There will be no more Private Members' time at any other time in the week. Ordinarily, in the Supply period they would get four hours per week; this ensures them three hours per week, or 40 hours in the first supply period. But since March 24, 1981 we have lost that time.
I want Members to be very clear about what they are giving up and to suggest that they give up that time for a year, to try it out and see if it improves things. I suspect our Special Committee might want to take another very hard look at that. Speaking as a Private Member, I feel I would give up that right most reluctantly when it comes to the confirmation or otherwise of this experiment a year from now.
I want to deal with the quorum for a moment. There have been some misguided souls who fancy themselves as experts on

November 29, 1982
Adjournment Motion
the procedures and practices of this place. They have published articles and/or editorials which conclude that the changes proposed with respect to the quorum would prevent forever more a repeat of the tactics that were employed to stop the energy omnibus Bill. Nothing could be further from the truth. As I understand it-and I am sure that it was the intention of the committee-it is a 15-minute bell so that the House sitting is not terminated simply because some over-zealous Member calls for a quorum when someone may be out having a coffee. It is meant to call a quorum together when our numbers fall below a quorum and we are considering some order of business. That is as far as the change goes, and I am happy to see the chairman of the committee nodding his head in agreement.
I think it is a great amendment in favour of the Government, but I would caution the Government that it should not become too lax as a result of having this luxury of a 15-minute bell and not have its Members in here to meet it. We have all seen in the last couple of weeks what can happen if the Government does not fulfil its responsibility to have a quorum here; the Speaker simply adjourns the House until the next day.
While I think of it, I also caution the Government, in its sincere effort at encouraging this kind of good faith of which all Parties speak in trying to make this experiment work, that it should also think twice before doing things without a quorum in the House.
Let me simply conclude by saying that we are accepting the third report with caution and on the understanding that the expectations inherent in the spirit of the report and spelled out in what the committee intends to address itself to in the future will be achieved. Unless there is substantial and meaningful reform which will restore to this place fiscal accountability, there can be no question of making these changes permanent. If we have the kind of meaningful reform which will restore to the people of Canada and their elected representatives through this institution the parliamentary control which must exist if democracy itself is to continue, then the changes in the third report have a chance of becoming permanent.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) does not get me wrong. I think it is an admirable change. One of its weaknesses is that we do not get current annual reports when they should be tabled. If that problem could be met, it would almost be a perfect change, were it not for the more serious one of the committee not being able to meet on its own initiative but relying on the Government to allow it to meet.
Let me just leave the Member with one example of the more serious problem. Under Standing Order 65(1 )(t) we now have a Standing Committee on Northern Pipelines which specifically has referred to it documents and papers under four specific sections of the Northern Pipeline Act. Despite repeated requests from the Opposition for that Standing Committee to meet since the beginning of this session, over two and a half years, it has not met because the Government has not allowed it to meet. Yet it is empowered specifically to look into specific papers that are required to be produced under a specific Act of Parliament. Without the ability to meet on its own initiative, the change is pretty meaningless.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to be able to speak on behalf of my Party this afternoon and also as a member of the Committee on Parliamentary Reform to the motion of the Government House Leader that the parliamentary reform package recommended by the third report of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure be adopted for the year 1983. I will try to do my best to match and transcend the enthusiasm which the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) demonstrated for the package. I look forward to hearing from other Members of his Party who will hopefully be more enthusiastic about what potential there is within this package for parliamentary reform, not just those reforms which are contained within the package but also those made possible down the road by the actions we are taking today. I will have more to say about that later.
I think we ought to stress, not in as tentative a way as the Opposition House Leader but in a positive way, that this is an experiment, that this is an interim report, and that these are the things the committee when it met thought it could come to an early consensus on and get before the House for its consideration. I am very pleased that we were able to do it, that we were able to put something before the House this fall, and that the three Party caucuses have had the wisdom to allow this to happen so quickly.
The adoption of this report by the House will break the ice on parliamentary reform. I am reminded of the ice that was
Parliamentary Reform
caked around my car when I arrived at the airport today. The experiment will break the ice on parliamentary reform and make other things more possible down the road.
Members of the committee know that the report is imperfect and that indeed there may be things we will find out as we go along which were overlooked. There will be unforeseen consequences of the reforms and other things which need to be straightened out as we go along. It might even be somewhat chaotic, but it will be a creative kind of chaos rather than the paralysing chaos to which we are so often treated in the House of Commons as it now operates. Whether or not the chaos is creative will depend upon whether the goodwill continues, the goodwill which made the unanimous report of the committee possible, which existed in the committee and exists in the House to the extent that we were able to come to an agreement to deal with it today and implement the experiment as of January, 1983.
There will have to be the will to make parliamentary reform actually work. This is why I hope there will be more enthusiasm on the part of the Official Opposition as a whole than I felt the Opposition House Leader demonstrated for the proposals. I do not think we ought to go into them on quite the tone he demonstrated, because I think it is very important for the life of Parliament and the life of the House of Commons, about which I know the Hon. Opposition House Leader cares, that we go into this area on as positive a note as possible.
If the goodwill breaks down and the Government decides not to call committees into existence to exercise their new powers, it will be a breach of faith for which the Government will be responsible. The Government will hear about it if it acts in such a way as to make these reforms unworkable. Many of the possibilities which are contained in this package will not actually come to fruition if the Government stands in the way, but I do not think the Government will do that. I certainly hope it will not. I do not think the Government would have agreed to these reforms if it were the Government's intention to stand in the way of allowing them to be given a real try. But only time will tell.
Adopting this report today is crucial in terms of looking down the road, in that it makes the rest of the committee's work more meaningful. In my view, it would have been very difficult for the committee to have carried on looking at very difficult issues; for instance, the speakership, the supply process and the whole question of accountability of the Government to Parliament for its expenditures. We could not have moved into this area as a committee had we not had the feeling that there was enough concern in the House for parliamentary reform to at least experiment with the package on which we are agreeing today.
I quite agree with those who have said that this is no radical reform. This is not something about which we should be beating our breasts all that loudly. But it is an important first step. It is not just a tentative step; it is a step about which we can feel a great deal of satisfacton. Nevertheless, we have to

November 29, 1982
Parliamentary Reform
see it for what it is. It is something that will break the psychology of despair about parliamentary reform which I have noticed, even being here only three and one-half years, has existed for some time, and particularly since the failure of the 1976 parliamentary reform committee. Thus, this is something from which we should take some satisfaction as a House of Commons today. This kind of opportunity presents itself so rarely, and 1 hope this is the beginning of something even more significant than the specific reforms that are contained within the package.
If we have difficulties down the line with recommendations that are in the package, committee members will be around to interpret the spirit of what the committee had in mind when it made its recommendations.
I hope the House Leaders and others who have to deal with the reality of these reforms will feel free to consult with members of the committee from time to time as to what we intended by this parliamentary reform, or to find out what was in our minds if we have not described it perfectly in the recommended Standing Orders.
This is one occasion for me, and I am sure for others on the committee, when I felt that Members of Parliament acting together could make a difference. In other words, Members of Parliament acting together made recommendations in such a way that the Government took steps to bring them into being.
One of the objects of parliamentary reform is that Members of Parliament can feel that they can make a difference when it comes to policy. We do, however, have a long way to go on that road. But 20 Members of Parliament got together, made recommendations and had them accepted, which means that a difference has been made. Therefore, we have given an example of what I would call parliamentary reform.
I think those who are concerned about things to come, as far as parliamentary reform is concerned, ought to take a look at the document that was mentioned, the so-called Huntington-Lachance position paper on accountability. It is called "Closing the Loop". This document is available to Members of Parliament and also to the public through the minutes of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure.
It seems to me that where the real problem lies is in making the Government more accountable to Members of Parliament for its actions. This is something which unites all Members of Parliament, regardless of the ideological differences that exist between Parties and individuals. We may want to make the Government accountable for different things. We do have different interests in what we want to pursue in terms of accountability, but it is in the interests of all Members of Parliament that the Government be made more accountable. That is certainly one of the most important areas with which the committee will deal. Adopting this report at this time will,
I hope, create the kind of momentum which will result in subsequent reports of the Special Committee being taken more seriously, instead of finding their way on to shelves to collect dust.
I do not intend to speak much longer but instead make myself available as a member of the committee for any questions that Hon. Members might have about what was intended by particular reforms. I must say I am somewhat disappointed that there are so few Hon. Members present for this discussion; it is a discussion since we do not expect a division on this matter. It is disappointing that there are so few Members around even to mark the occasion. When I subtract members of the committee who are present here in the House from the total number of Hon. Members present in the Chamber, it seems that not very many Members hunger and thirst for more knowledge of what the committee had in mind with its recommendations.
The first few sections of the recommendations in the report have to do with the parliamentary calendar and timetable. To a great extent, that has been gone over. The parliamentary timetable is important in lending a degree of predictability to the planning of Members of Parliament. However, this does not only apply to Members of Parliament; it lends predictability in terms of timing to the political process and to the lives of everyone connected with the political process and with the life of Parliament. I think this particular reform will be beneficial and I am looking forward to seeing how it works out. The parliamentary timetable, however, is not particularly contentious.
I do want to speak about the length of speeches and the proposal within the report to curtail speeches to 20 minutes. Speeches previously were given a time limit of 40 minutes. If I use 40 minutes, Mr. Speaker, it is because I am taking advantage of my last opportunity to do so. Speeches which were formerly 40 minutes in length will now be reduced to 20 minutes, to be followed by a ten-minute question period.
The object of this change is to restore to Parliament, in a structured way, actual debate. There was a feeling among witnesses who came before the committee that the Commons was being treated to a constant string of set speeches and there was not enough cut and thrust back and forth between Members. By adding on this ten-minute exchange period Members might deliver the kinds of speeches which they could defend in a subsequent ten-minute question and answer session. We would also have the opportunity for more genuine debate.
This is another example of reform that will depend on two factors. One is the way Members use the debate and the custom which develops from this debate. The other factor concerns the discretion of the Chair. I, or I believe anyone else on the committee, do not foresee a Member rising to speak for nine out of the ten minutes in a rebuttal while the Member who originally spoke would only have a minute to reply. The purpose is for a Member to make a brief comment or ask a brief question, which could happen perhaps as many as four times within that ten-minute period in response to comments or questions which may have been raised during another Member's speech. I believe that that was what the committee
November 29, 1982

was considering. It was not simply to replace 40-minute speeches with 20-minute speeches that were interspersed with 10-minute speeches. The purpose was to alow time for real debate.
I also want to comment on Standing Order 43. This was a difficult subject for the committee to deal with. We probably spent more time on this than we did on the other questions. We felt that the difficulty with motions under Standing Order 43 was public perception of them, especially since the proceedings of the House of Commons are now televised. These motions are incomprehensible to many people watching. Some of the motions which are moved during that 15-minute period before Question Period debase the language of "urgent and pressing necessity". As well, the requests for unanimous consent and the denial of that unanimous consent, particularly when motions were worded in such a way as to be obviously acceptable, gave the impression that Parliament was being negative toward quite otherwise positive statements made by Members. Therefore, we felt that the entire concept of Standing Order 43 needed to be reformed.
We considered what the actual purpose of motions under Standing Order 43 was. We felt that Members needed an opportunity to bring their concerns about particular issues of the day before the House on a regular daily basis. What eventually happened on motions under Standing Order 43 was that this Standing Order became the vehicle by which these concerns were expressed. The kernel, the importance of these motions is that they allow Members the opportunity to put themselves on record on a regular basis and bring to the attention of other Members, the House, their constituents and the country their opinions on particular issues or on the Government's performance.
We hope that this period of Members' statements will accomplish this better. It will be interesting to see how it works. There will be fewer statements than motions under Standing Order 43, but I hope that these statements will be more substantial. I am looking forward to that.
Real reform will continue to occur only if this mood for reform which presently exists continues and the work of the committee continues, and the House remains receptive to its subsequent reports.
I do not think this is an experiment which is overwhelmingly in favour of the Government. I disagree with the Opposition House Leader in that respect. 1 believe it is a balanced report. We discussed many of the matters which were raised by the Opposition House Leader. We reviewed all of those arguments as an all-Party committee. We came up with these recommendations and agreed that it was a fair package. 1 hope we can approach it in that light. Since the Government bears a great deal of responsibility, we hope that it will continue in good faith and that we will be able sometime to look back at this change and see this day as the beginning of more significant reforms in the Canadian House of Commons.
In keeping with what I said previously, if there are Members who wish to ask me questions about the committee's report, I
Parliamentary Reform
will not yield my time until it is clear that there are no Members who wish to ask questions. In that case, I will assume that I have overwhelmed them with my remarks and that no more needs to be said. I also look forward to hearing from the chairman of the committee since I understand he is next to speak.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Now that we have completed the first round of speakers, one speaker per Party, I believe there is an agreement between all sides of the House that we have a 15-minute time limit. There was an agreement to exempt the chairman and the vice-chairman from that time limit, but they have volunteered to accept the 15-minute time limit to demonstrate their great desire for shorter speeches. I believe the House will agree.

Mr. Speaker, I looked over to see whether the chairman of the committee, the Hon. Member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre), was agreeable to be bound. He is. Therefore, I and my Party are agreeable.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Subsequent speeches in this debate will be limited to 15 minutes. Agreed and so ordered.

Mr. Speaker, I am very proud, today, to have this opportunity of taking part in the debate on the third report of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure. I greatly appreciated the kind words spoken on my behalf by the Government House Leader and the House Leader of the Official Opposition. Instead of elaborating on the report's recommendations, I would prefer to take this opportunity to explain the Committee's approach to its mandate, to point out the general direction of the reforms and to outline the Committee's agenda for the coming months.
The Committee started its work rather tentatively, with a first meeting in July. Although all Committee members favoured reform, it was clear that Hon. Members did not have the same views on what the Committee's agenda should be. Some wondered which questions should become the focus of immediate reform, and how much time should be spent on this by the Committee. Committee members also wondered whether they should be informing the general public about the role of Canada's Parliament. Subsequently, the Committee tried to project its ideas on reform. During our initial proceedings, we held internal discussions, without witnesses, about our own perceptions of the need for reform and how we perceived the various roles that all Hon. Members and Parliament play in the daily lives of Canadians. Later, we listened with interest to a number of expert witnesses, all of whom made invaluable

November 29, 1982
Parliamentary Reform
contributions, although I would like to mention a few whose participation was particulary appreciated, especially in the production of the report before the House today.
Representatives of the Canadian Bar Association were the first witnesses to appear before the Committee, and they helped us to clarify our concepts of parliamentary reform. Dr. John Stewart of St. Francis Xavier University gave us the benefit of his knowledge, not only as an academic but also as a former member of this House. Justice James Jerome, former Speaker of the House, helped us to put our ideas in their proper perspective. However, we owe a special debt of gratitude to a former Clerk of the House, Mr. Alistair Fraser. Mr. Fraser appeared before the Committee and gave us such excellent ideas that we asked him if he would give us the benefit of his services by becoming Special Adviser to the Committee. The changes in the Standing Orders that will become effective as of December 22 of this year, as recommended by the Committee, reflect the quality of his advice and the appreciation of his suggestions.
I should also like to mention our Senior Clerk, Mr. Robert Marleau, who helped a great deal in planning the Committee's work and organizing the support staff, which did a tremendous job. Mr. Philip Laundy and all the Library of Parliament staff provided invaluable and very substantial assistance. Mr. Speaker, when the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) announced in June that this Committee would be formed, he was keeping his word, because I remember clearly that as soon as he was appointed Government House Leader, he came out in favour of parliamentary reform and announced that he intended to start the process during his first term. The fact that we have now approved the Committee's recommendations demonstrates that he was sincere. That is entirely to his credit, and I am pleased to offer him my sincere congratulations.
Mr. Speaker, when my colleagues on the Government side asked me to chair the Committee's proceedings, I knew I was taking on an extraordinary challenge. I admit that I thought about it for some time before I accepted, not because I was intimidated by the challenge, but because I wanted to be sure that all parties were taking seriously the need to change our Standing Orders and procedures. As we all know, Parliament is going through a very difficult period and our credibility is at stake. It was therefore not unreasonable to wonder whether it was possible to find twenty members representing the three parties in the House, a team that would be able to reach a consensus so that the Committee could table a unanimous, serious report with realistic recommendations, with the hope of gaining the approval of all parties so that the recommendations could be implemented in the near future.
Mr. Speaker, I soon realized that all three parties were serious and sincere when I saw the list of Hon. Members sitting on the Committee. My nineteen colleagues on the Committee reflect, 1 believe, the aspirations of Canadians from all parts of this country and include a number of former ministers, experienced members of Parliament and also newly elected members. This is a splendid team. I am very grateful to them, first of all for having elected me as Chairman of the
Committee and second, I am grateful for their sincerity, their dedication and their commitment. The fact that the Committee's report has met with the approval of all parties in this House proves that Committee members have done an extraordinary job, and they deserve the congratulations of all their colleagues. I also wish to mention the invaluable assistance I received from the Committee's two Vice-Chairmen, the first being my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), former minister in the Progressive Conservative Government.
This Hon. Member showed on many occasions that he could rise above political partisanship and demonstrate his love and respect for this institution in helping us arrive at these recommendations. It was personally rewarding to me to have the opportunity of working with him.
I would also like to mention the great help brought to the committee by the knowledge of the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans). It was important that our recommendations reflect the concerns of the third Party and his interventions assured this to the committee. Both of the Hon. Members helped to make my task much easier. This report reflects their commitment as well as that of all the other Members.
I would like to make special mention of the constant presence and participation of the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), who was not a member but attended every meeting and participated. After hearing witnesses, we spent some time allowing members of the committee to restate their concerns with regard to reform. During this process, it became evident to me that we were beginning to function, not as a committee made up of partisan MPs, but rather as Parliamentarians concerned about the health of this institution. We all had a common goal of effecting meaningful and constructive changes in an atmosphere of collegiality and based on consensus. The attendance of the members of this committee was well above the norm in all my years of experience here, and their interventions in debate always had a very high standard. Again, I wish to stress the fact that the House has benefited because the people on the committee acted as Members of Parliament and not as representatives of political parties. I am amazed at the great quantity and high quality of work which can be done when this is the case.
The first series of meetings allowed us to identify the issues of reform. We then realized in subsequent meetings that there were certain reforms which could be implemented immediately while others would require further study and perhaps the summoning of further witnesses. We determined that it was important to have a beginning to the reform process and, for that reason, submitted the report and committed ourselves to subsequent reports to follow.
November 29, 1982

The changes suggested in the report, while allowing the Government to govern, addressed the balance which must be maintained to enable a Member of Parliament effectively to represent the electorate. These reforms will enhance the role of the Member in the House of Commons debates and in the committee system as well.
I would like to mention briefly some of the recommendations. The first is with reference to the fixed dates for sittings or the parliamentary calendar. Finally we will know and, more importantly, Canadians will know when their Parliament is in session. After 115 or 116 years, the Canadian people will know. The parliamentary calendar will enable all of us, whether in Government or in Opposition, to plan our activities more rationally and effectively.
Concerning the item on the length of speeches, the committee feels that the implementation of the recommendation of shorter speeches with a short debate following will greatly help in making this forum more lively and, especially, more relevant.
With regard to the subject of committee reform, it has long been felt by most of us that the committee system needed revamping, and quickly. Our proposals point the way in helping to make the role of the PM more meaningful and important through committee work.
I would like to draw attention to the fact that, with regard to the future, we in the committee view this report as only a beginning, yet a very important and meaningful beginning. I would like to assure Hon. Members that we are still working and have committed ourselves to at least two or three further reports.
The section of the report dealing with the future does list a number of matters with which the committee will be dealing as its meetings continue. The future report of the committee will deal with the issue of accountability. Two of our Members have tabled a report on that matter and we are studying what has been referred to as the Huntington/Lachance report, which shows the quality of the work that can be accomplished within this type of committee. This will focus on the relevant aspects of ministerial, administrative and financial responsibility.
The structure of the committee system will also be studied. This will involve items such as the introduction of a panel of chairmen, administrative budgets for committees and the possibility of minority reports. While the position of the Private Member has been considerably enhanced by the present recommendations, the committee will continue to deal with this subject.
The institution of the Speakership will form the subject of a special report. Attention will be directed to the planning of the legislative agenda and non-controversial legislation.
Once again, I wish to thank all members of the committee for their excellent work, the three Party House Leaders and all Hon. Members of this House, for without their support, no matter how excellent our work, the House would not have given its unanimous approval, which it did. Unanimous
Parliamentary Reform
acceptance was crucial in having its recommendations implemented. I recognize, as well, the importance of the support given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent), and this is also to their credit.
In conclusion and in keeping with the recommendation in the report, if any of my colleagues wish to question me-and I notice that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) made the same offer-I will be pleased to answer those questions that I am able to answer, with Your Honour's permission.

Mr. Speaker, I want first of all to thank the Hon. Member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre) for his kind wishes and extremely kind sentiments expressed towards me and, of course, towards the other members of the committee, but I speak personally now and want to thank him very much. I want to reciprocate by saying that, under his chairmanship, this committee has for me been one of the happiest experiences of my parliamentary life which extends, as does that of many other Members, over some ten years.
I think it is fair to say that the committee was successful in many ways because its presiding officer, the chairman of the committee, was not wont to stand on Members, was able to give Members sufficient time to express themselves, did not come to his work in the chair with preconceived notions, but, more than that, brought years of experience and understanding of how this place works to bear on the work that we were given by the terms of reference.
I want to say that if we have been successful-certainly there has been co-operation among the members of the committee-it is because there has been great leadership by the chairman of the committee, and I am sure that my colleagues on all sides of the House of Commons would want to share in that sentiment.
Hear, hear!

I am pleased that he mentioned the support that has been given to parliamentary reform by the Leaders of the Parties, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), and the Hon. Member for Oshawa, the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent). I think it is fair to say that the Party Leaders have given their support to parliamentary reform.
I think it is appropriate that at the beginning of my speech I pay tribute to the Leader of the Opposition. The House Leader of the Government (Mr. Pinard) paid tribute to his Leader. It was the Leader of the Opposition who, in the campaign in 1979 and in his first term as Prime Minister of Canada, indicated two commitments: the reform of the Parliament of Canada, hopefully; secondly, the question of openness in Government.

November 29, 1982
Parliamentary Reform
I was honoured with the responsibility of leading in the preparation of the position paper on parliamentary reform in 1979, with the backing of the then Prime Minister; and I also had the privilege of introducing in this House the first freedom of information legislation in the Parliament of Canada introduced by a Government, which I also remember with great affection. I see my friend across the aisle smiling, but I do remember it with great affection and long to return to the opportunity of introducing legislation. In any event, it was a commitment by my Party Leader to those issues that allowed that to be done very early, and I think that is important and hope the House will understand if 1 say that our Party has been known as the Party of reform in terms of this institution.
The next thing 1 would like to mention is the work of Mr. Alistair Fraser, the officers of the Table, the people from the Library of Parliament and all of the staff of this Parliament who have been so helpful to us. They have really been a strong rod and staff.
I would like to say to my own House Leader, the Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), that many of the reservations that he has expressed, as House Leaders of Oppositions are wont to do-I can say that now because I am no longer the House Leader of the Opposition-are reservations that were expressed in the committee which were dealt with and put aside.
We recognized in the committee that just as the committee itself would fail if the members of that committee did not act in good faith, so the whole process of reform would fail if the Government, Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition and the third Party in the House of Commons did not act in good faith. Men can devise rules from now until the Second Coming and there will never be a set of rules that will encompass the concerns of all people on all sides of the House of Commons. 1 am not commenting on the validity of those concerns because those are always concerns; they are legitimate reservations that one has. But one can take a look at the rules of this House, of the British House, of the American Congress and the Australian House of Representatives and one can find gaping loopholes in those rules. They run there on good faith. If the place is to run at all, it will run on good faith. If this experiment is to be successful-because that is what it is-it will have to be carried out in good faith, and the burden of the failure will lie on the heads of those who do not act in good faith.
The committee understood that they were embarking on a bit of a new voyage in terms of this report. I want to say to the House that there was an understanding among all the members of that committee that Governments have certain responsibilities, Governments must get a legislative program through-or should get a legislative program through. The public will judge whether that legislative program is good or bad. But Members of Parliament, the Opposition certainly but Members of Parliament on all sides of the House who do not form the executive, who are not members of the Cabinet, have to have the tools by which they can examine what Governments are doing.
1 believe there is more to this House of Commons than merely saying yes or no to what Government proposes. I think there is much more to this place than what is contained in those epithets that one hears-the "trained seals", the "sheep" and so on. I believe there is much more to it than that. Not only should we, in a modern democracy, be able to vote yes or no to sustain a Government or not; surely we have to have the tools to ask the questions why and why not?
If the purpose of Parliament is anything, it is to allow Members of Parliament who are not in the Government to do much more than just dispose of what Government brings to Parliament. It is much more than that. Surely it is to ask those questions, to inquire, to let Government propose on the one hand, but to be able to inquire without hindrance into the merit of what it proposes on the other. It is this sense of balance that I have tried to put to the House that occupied the work of the committee.
I want to say that we as a committee have not regarded this report as the last word in parliamentary reform. It is the first word in parliamentary reform. It is the first word that has been adopted out of the unanimous report without any changes whatsoever. That is historical, I believe at least in your time, Mr. Speaker, and your time extends back for some period. I will not say how long. 1 think that is something for all of us to remember. It puts a tremendous burden on all of us.
The Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill said that the purpose of this first work is to break the ice. 1 say it is a log jam. It is hopefully to bring an end to what has been written about in learned journals as a crisis in confidence in the Parliament of Canada. The people are looking at our political institutions, and they are looking at them with a sense of cynicism. They say they are not representative. They say Governments can do what they want without hindrance. They say that the Member is bound by the Party line; he can never speak as he would like to speak, he must always vote the Party line. Our committee has indicated that the very fundamental matter of confidence is something that is going to be looked at in the future section of the report. We look, as a committee, at the independent references to committees, using the techniques which have been described by the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mr. Lachance), as the way in which Parliament can get out from under the thumb of government. It seems to me that whether the government is Conservative, Liberal, or New Democratic, if the latter should ever happen, it does not make much difference in the parliamentary system. Members of Parliament have been heretofore under the thumb of government in terms of what they can do and what they cannot do, what they can investigate and what they cannot investigate.
I believe it is in keeping with the parliamentary system that further power be granted to the House. If Governments act improperly in granting this power, if they do not call committees, then there is going to be one devil of a political price to pay. On the other hand, in the use of that power, if Members of Parliament, in the Opposition, perhaps, or anywhere else,
November 29, 1982

act irresponsibly, then there is going to be a political price to pay. Obstruction heretofore has been the only real weapon that an Opposition has, and that is what has happened to the system. I put it to you that as we develop these rules, the Opposition will still have the legitimate use of obstruction. It is still there. But what we as a committee hope is that there will be provided some other weapons as well, the weapons of legitimate inquiry, of independence, and we hope that as our work goes forward we will have further resources.
The work of this Committee, Mr. Speaker, has just begun. Every one of us, Liberal, Conservative, New Democrat, Independent, if we believe in this Parliament we have to give this experiment an honest try. We will be worried about how it proceeds, naturally. It is an experiment, but it is the first time when we can perhaps begin to turn this crisis around.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to commend to every Member of this House that they read very carefully the future section of this Report, and I want to say to the Government House Leader that I believe it is important that this Committee stay together for the length of this experiment. This Committee that has worked so well together, should stay together and continue to work. I believe that is important to the success of the experiment, in order to bring about the whole change which the House Leader for the Opposition spoke about. I want to thank my hon. friends for the privilege of serving on that Committee. I hope the Government will allow it to continue so that we will be able to begin the second step of bringing this institution out of some of the chaos and crisis.

Mr. Speaker, I must admit it is a great pleasure for me to participate in this discussion this afternoon, particularly to follow the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker). I say that in all sincerity because there have been two very pleasant experiences in my ten years in Ottawa; one was the time we spent on the Fiscal Transfer Payments Committee, and the other one was the time we spent on the committee discussing the change to the House regulations.
That is because I was on both of them.

And I must admit that the hon. gentleman for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), who participated on both committees, made it particularly enjoyable. In all sincerity, one of the reasons I enjoyed those two committees was that the attitude of the Members was non-partisan. It was an attempt to accomplish as much as possible in a non-partisan fashion. As a result of that, the work of those two committees has born fruit. In the case of the committee studying the changes to the regulations, of course, all we have brought in at the moment is an interim report. I believe that the major work of the committee has yet to be accomplished. I say this because, and I see across the floor of the House, the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), I believe that the tough stuff, the difficult work, the discussions of how we are going to change the rules as they relate to accountability, are still to come. I know this is
Parliamentary Reform
not likely to result in the same consensus as we have had up to date. However, my purpose is not to speak of what is to come, but to speak of what we have done so far.
I must admit that, as do all Members of the Committee, I have certain reservations on some of the items on which we have reached a consensus. I did say, for example, in a somewhat lighter vein, that I was concerned about what we were going to be doing with our evenings in the future when we were not working in the House or on Committees, although I have been assured the Government is going to find something to keep us out of mischief. Nevertheless, there were certain other aspects on which individual Members were not necessarily in agreement. I wondered if we were wise to devote Wednesday afternoon entirely to Private Members' Business. However, it is on this particular subject that I want to address my remarks this afternoon.
We have not yet come to the stage of discussing how best to use the amount of time that is allocated to the individual Members of this House of Commons, and I do want to express my opinion that this is one of the decisions which the Committee is going to have to reach at a fairly early stage, a recommendation on the basis on which the Members will be able to bring their representations to the floor of the House for decision of the Members. I say this in all sincerity. It is not the decision of the Government, it is the decision of the Members. We have to be able to bring our representations forth in a fashion in which we can have what I would term a "free" vote. Thus I proposed to the Committee, through my own brief, as most Members submitted their individual briefs, that we find some means by which we can make Private Members' Hour more meaningful. As many Members will be aware, I have a habit of standing up here at five o'clock on a Thursday afternoon and attempting to use up one hour or part of one hour of Private Members' time. I do not do this with any great pleasure. I must admit I do it because I have some representation to make, but I also do it because we do not have a mechanism at the present time by which we can come to a decision on an issue without putting the Government in a difficult position. In other words, the Government has to suggest to its Members that they have to vote against a particular motion when the public might assume that it would make a lot more sense to vote in favour of the subject matter.
My suggestion, for what it is worth, is that we should find some mechanism by which representations of individual Members can go to a special committee for study. The committee would then report back to the House, not necessarily in the same form as the Hon. Member's original representation, but would report back to the House in a fashion that has been well considered, possibly after the calling of witnesses, and at that stage, the report would be subject to debate. The report itself would then probably lead to a vote. Since the vote would not be binding on the Government, I see this as probably one of the easiest ways to get a free expression of opinion amongst the Members of this House.

Parliamentary Reform
Now, I have talked on this particular point to illustrate, as my good friend, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) said, that the work of the committee has only just started. We have a long way to go, and this is one of the items discussed briefly and put aside because it will mean lengthy discussions before we arrive at a consensus. But it must be abundantly clear to everyone who looks at the new rules that putting together three Private Members' Hours on a Wednesday afternoon does not resolve the present difficulty of private Members' representations being generally of little value except for putting in a mailer to illustrate to the Member's constituents his own point of view on a particular subject. At some point we must face the need to bring the issue to the floor of the House for decision by all Members.
The same applies in many other areas. I spoke of accountability, but everyone knows we have also discussed amongst ourselves the personal issues, personal to Members of Parliament, as to how we should govern our own affairs. In other words, we have discussed the manner in which the choice of the speaker should be decided. These are things on which we have to reach a decision and on which, I hope, the consensus of Members of the committee will be sought in future reports.
As is generally known, it is our intention to look at the operation of other legislative bodies, particularly Westminster, which is essentially the pattern on which we operate here. We hope to gain from them some additional wisdom from which to make further recommendations to the House. It is not my intention to delve in depth into the problems facing our committee, but only to say that I was so delighted with the attitude of the Members in the deliberations so far that I am encouraged, probably for the first time in my nine years here-maybe I should say for the second time because I was also encouraged by the non-partisan attitude on the committee concerned with transfer payments-because I saw 20 individual Members who were able to pursue a consensus through freely expressing their point of view in a non-partisan fashion. We had an objective. We all recognized that the House as it is presently operating is not functioning satisfactorily. We recognized that the public had an image of the House which made us less than proud of the part we were playing in its operation. With that objective in mind, we decided that we had to bring forth some meaningful changes which would encourage the public to have a little more confidence in their legislative body.
I will conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying how pleased I was to participate in the discussions, and how happy I am that we were able to come to a consensus on so many wide and different subjects, and present to the House a unanimous report. I think that in itself was a tremendous achievement. I hope and pray that in future deliberations of this committee which, as the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton says, must continue- and I hope this point has been well made to Government; no matter what happens when this session ends, no matter what time this session ends, we honestly believe that committee must continue in the same spirit in order to ensure our legislative body is able to convey to the public that, apart from the
normal partisanship which must exist between the Government and Opposition, there is a spirit on the part of all Members of this House to ensure that it makes some sense and that it is something of which we can all be proud. We want the public to feel that this is a good body of people they have sent to Ottawa to do their job, and in that regard they are satisfied with the way in which we operate.
As I have set out to convey, Mr. Speaker, we have a lot of work to do. I feel a lot has been accomplished. I would like publicly to express my appreciation to my colleagues on the committee for the enjoyable meetings we had, and the fact that we were able to reach a consensus. It is also my hope that the same spirit will continue in our future deliberations.

Mr. Speaker, I am very honoured to participate in this debate, in particular because I am not a member of the committee concerned, yet I have read the third report of the committee and its nine recommendations for fundamental change. While I quite approve of the concerns expressed by my House Leader on some of the implications of these changes, as only time will tell, I certainly do agree with my friend, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), the Vice-Chairman of the committee, that this is certainly an historic day when the report of a committee on procedure is to be unanimously adopted by this House. My House Leader is here and can well reflect on the last committee concerned with the change of rules, which is referred to briefly in the report. It was a tremendously different mood then compared to what it is today, because the last changes were forced on the House by closure brought on by the now resurrected Mr. Macdonald, Chairman of the Royal Commission on the Economy. I well remember the prolonged debate, and in fact closure was invoked in a hot July. I agree with all Members who have spoken today about the tremendous difference in attitude today when this experimentation in effect is agreed on by all Members with the full knowledge that there may be some imperfections or dilemmas not fully seen by the committee, but at least it is a first step.
I agree completely, Mr. Speaker, with something said by the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton. It certainly has been my experience around here, that is, that you can pervert and prostitute any rule or procedure you want if you do not have good faith and a little understanding of each other's point of view. I think that is one of the things which affected, adversely, the work of the last committee on procedure, of which I was happy to be a member and which was chaired by Mr. Sharp, the then Government House Leader. We travelled to England, we did everything that all committees do, and we came up with many interim reports, and of course nothing was ever adopted because we got bogged down in a real partisan atmosphere where the work of that committee went for naught. I think we had some type of report in 1976 and nothing ever came of it.
In this case, Mr. Speaker, I am bemused and frankly amazed that this committee, with its 20 members, could come up with an objective report and get agreement on recommending to their respective caucuses agreement on the report so that
November 29, 1982

it could come before this House as a unanimous recommendation of the three Parties. I do not know really what the reason for that is, whether we are prepared to agree on an experiment because we know we are more than half way through this session and change for a year will not affect too much as long as it is provisional and experimental; or whether it is the reading of the polls, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps it is the more willingly receptive nature of Government Members to experiment with rule changes. The idea could be that after another election the positions could be reversed. They could be sitting to the left of the Speaker, wanting certain changes. Frankly, no matter on which side of the House one sits, there is agreement that the rules do constipate Members in the discharge of their duties.
Regardless of the reasons for this, Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to participate in the debate in the 15 minutes allocated to me, recognizing the admonition of my House Leader that in the next session the good faith exhibited by members of the committee be continued. It has to be continued, Mr. Speaker, and I think it can be, because of the calibre of members of that committee. I think they can influence their House Leaders.
As has been indicated in the speeches we have heard today, I firmly believe that the changes to the rules of the House of Commons are not changes to the rules of a House Leader or the rules of a Party, but to the rules of the Members.
I was disappointed that I was not a member of that committee but unfortunately, all the Members from this Party were very diligent in their attendance and their contribution, so I could not sneak in the back door. I will remedy that on another day. Because of their diligence I hope that we succeed with this experiment. It is a first step, a break in the logjam. We all know that although one can break a logjam, that still does not get the logs to market; there can be many back eddies or rocks and obstructions before the logs get to market.
I hope against hope that the good work of the committee and all the interesting experiments that will take place in the next year, will end in the adoption of these changes.
Even more fundamental than the good work that has been done on the issue of accountability, is the matter of votes of confidence in this House. This was touched upon by the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) and the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton. We can tinker around with the rules with all the goodwill in the world, but we must meet the issue of accountability, which is the reason the House of Commons was created all those years ago. Indeed, the reason for this Chamber being green is to represent the meadow in which the barons met behind the bullrushes, so that the King could not see them meeting and planning to resist his authority. All that is history, but accountability is fundamental today when even the Auditor General says that spending is out of control.
Speaking as a private Member, something that I think is even more fundamental than accountability, is a change in the rules as they relate to votes of confidence. There are many reasons why this change is forced upon us. It is overdue. One element has not been touched upon today, although it was
Parliamentary Reform
perhaps part of the deliberations of the committee, and that is that before another election there could be 28 new Members in this House. I will not get into the pros and cons of that issue, but I believe that the larger this institution becomes, the more fundamental is its reform. It is important that through Private Members' Hour, or through Members acting collectively or acting privately but without Party Whips, it should be possible to influence the legislative process.
It is as clear as it is that the sky is blue over Nova Scotia all the time, and as it is that it is sometimes foggy in Vancouver, that as the base of the legislature is expanded-be that in England with 485 Members, be it Russia with the Soviet Socialist Republics and Members coming off the steppes, the Urals or Siberia-the larger the institution the more powerful the executive becomes, regardless of its political stripe.
It is for that reason that I am glad we are discussing some of the nine changes. I will not go into detail on all of them as we will have a chance to experiment with them and get into the details in the next session.
I could talk about the paradoxes of this place, Mr. Speaker. As I said in the brief that I sent to the Committee, never have there been more people coming to the House, never have more people been able to see the House through the means of television, but also never has the House or its Members been more out of the touch with the public.
Another paradox should force change, and if it does not, then this place is terminally ill. I think Members of the Committee recognized that because they came up with some changes, but not the one with which I want to deal now. The other paradox which forces change is that it is now a full-time job to be a Member of Parliament. I come from the East, other Members come from distant places in the West and from Central Canada, but regardless of where we come from, this is a full-time job. I am very happy to consider some type of parliamentary timetable. Jesus Christ taught in parables but 1 like to teach in paradoxes.
This institution is supposed to organize the business of Government and the business of the country but until a parliamentary timetable was suggested, we could not even organize our own time. That was an ironic paradox, I think. We are paid on the basis of a full-time occupation. Even though we may be pseudo-celebrities because of television and may have some status in our ridings, because of the different lifestyle necessitated by travelling back and forth to Ottawa, there are difficulties.
No matter how many improvements have been introduced since 1 became a Member-and I give full credit to the Government for the improvement in research facilities, constituency offices, technological change and travel privileges- there is no substitute for the physical presence of the Member in the House. That is a fundamental lesson that I have learned since becoming a Member. Members must be able to have a focus in their ridings so that their constituents can feel they have an opportunity to contribute to the legislative process and are not just taking part in a charade.

November 29, 1982
Parliamentary Reform
In many ways we are nobodies, Mr. Speaker. I believe that is a philosophical question which could be debated. I certainly believe that Members of the British Parliament are nobodies, unless they sit in Cabinet or in the shadow cabinet of the Opposition front bench. That is England.
My time has almost expired, Mr. Speaker. I am very glad that everyone complied with the 15-minute rule, after the opening round. The most fundamental question that Members who speak later could touch upon is the matter of votes of confidence. Ironically, the issues of the day have already caused us to experiment with that. There are some issues that carry no Party label-capital punishment, marijuana, abortion-and are social issues, matters of conscience. When Mr. Pearson was Prime Minister he experimented with a vote of confidence in theory and it was basically carried out in practice-a free vote.
This question should not be put off, Mr. Speaker. The Committee brought in a third report, but it will fail this House and the public if in its next mandate it does not address the question of a two-tier system of votes of confidence. I submit that if a Government loses a vote on the Throne Speech, a Budget or on tax Bills, it should then definitely fall. The Prime Minister should tell his Members they must support the Government or else take to the hustings. No Member likes to go out on the hustings; there is a possibility of being stricken by a terminal disease. On the other hand, on Bills such as those affecting unemployment insurance, medicare, Canada Day, Dominion Day, the railways or air transport, if the Government loses the vote, the next statement made by the Chair should be to the effect that "Bill so-and-so has been defeated. Has the Government lost the confidence of the House?" In 999 cases out of 1,000 the Government would not have lost the confidence of the House, but there would have been a clear direction from all Members for the Bill to be amended and then brought back to the House where it would get the support from all Members. That is as it should be.
Agreed!
Hear, hear!

Why should we continue to vote as was done in the days of John A. Macdonald? We are being paid a good salary and are given benefits, yet the vote is conducted as it was 100-odd years ago.
There is much more that I would like to say, Mr. Speaker, but I will conclude by saying that I believe this first step for procedural reform could become the proverbial procedural leap for the Canadian Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I was wondering whether the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) would clarify a point that he made in the first part of his speech. He said that the last major rule changes in the House of Commons came about as a result of the implication of Standing Order 33. I was under the
impression that it was only one part of those changes which applied to Standing Order 33, and that the rules changes report was accepted unanimously, with the exception of the change proposed to set up the time allocations proposals under Standing Order 75.

Mr. Speaker, I would be glad to respond to the Hon. Member who I know at that time was a very valuable member of the committee. He will also know from his work in the committee that he is quite correct. I was here during the whole debate and I believe, if the Hon. Member really wants the history, that it was the first speech of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) wherein he invoked closure to get some closure under Standing Order 75A, 75B or 75C, but I can tell him that the temper in the halls and the temper in the House of Commons was nothing like the temper here today.

AFTER RECESS

At 8 p.m. the House resumed.

The last Hon. Member speaking before eight o'clock was the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan). I understand he has completed his remarks. Seeing that we have a quorum in the House, I am delighted to recognize next the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith).

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in this debate. I consider it an honour to have served on this Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure. I wish to outline a few brief points and make some observations about the report we have before us today. However, before doing that 1 would like to pay tribute to the good leadership that we have had on this committee. In particular, I would like to mention the Chairman, the Vice-Chairmen, Mr. Alistair Fraser and also those connected with the Table who helped us in many ways.
I think this report is a good one. It is an objective and a balanced report. I think it will help to make this place function better and work more efficiently. I have a few points that I would like to make but I will try to follow the example we hope to set in the next little while and give a short speech.
First, it is important to bear in mind that Members on this committee approached their task as parliamentarians. They did not come with the mind-set of an Opposition Member or of a Government Member. Perhaps at our first three meetings there was an inclination on the part of some people to do that. I may have succumbed to the temptation to do that myself, but any attitude that Members had along that line evaporated fairly quickly.
November 29, 1982

The committee made a wise choice in deciding to go out of town on two occasions. We went away for three days on one occasion, and on another occasion for two days. We worked together, we ate together, we set Party differences aside, and I think we developed some camaraderie. I believe the report that we have before us here is proof and evidence of the fact that parliamentarians, regardless of Party, can in fact work together to help make the House function better. The first point to bear in mind is that this report is the work of parliamentarians who worked together as parliamentarians.
Second, what we have here is a balanced package. I suppose the temptation is always there to go through a report like this and say that 1 like this and I do not like that. We will support this but not that because this will help us and that does not. That sort of thing leads to people picking and choosing. I have to commend the House Leaders and the Leaders of all Parties in the House because they did not succumb to that temptation. They accepted to advice of the members of this Committee that this was a balanced package.
Let us take an example. I suppose some people could argue that when the time limit for speeches is reduced, considerably in some instances, that will in the long run perhaps help the Government in that it will speed up the pace with which legislation is dealt. I suppose to some extent that is true. But, on the other hand, by having the Government agree to a fixed annual schedule it loses what has traditionally been a very important tool, one which governments of both Parties have used in the past. For example, when it is near Christmas or early summer the Government can say to the Opposition, "We will not give you a specific date, but here is a list of a certain number of Bills." The Government can say to the Opposition that when those Bills have been disposed of in a reasonable way, the House will adjourn. That is an important and powerful tool for the Government. The Government has given up that tool, and I am pleased it has. In return, however, we will have shorter speeches. That is an example of the way in which this report is balanced.
Third, I think this report will go a long way to making the role of a Member of Parliament more meaningful. Smaller committees will mean that a Member will serve on fewer committees, but the individual will be expected to become more familiar with the subject matter with which the committee deals. By having annual reports automatically going to standing committees, Members of Parliament will be able to get their teeth into the whole question of policy development in a way which they really have not been able to do in their review of the Estimates. Perhaps a lenient chairman might allow that under the current system, but 1 suggest that does not happen too often. We will find this is something that can and will happen, and it is a good thing.
To some extent we are going in the American direction, but not in a way that will allow fishing expeditions. We are going in the American direction in a way that will help bring the Government and the bureaucracy under greater scrutiny by elected officials. In my opinion, that is good.
Parliamentary Reform
Fourth, the adoption of this report will make Parliament more practical and more readily understandable to the public. Let me give a few personal examples, of which a quorum is one. I suppose that I will not be able to close down an Opposition emergency debate any more, as I once did on that famous night you will recall, Mr. Speaker. But that is fine. I am happy to see that surrendered. I do not think that it was-

speechtext: Sneaky.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
