It was not sneaky. I was just using the Standing Orders.
I believe that these recommendations are practical and desirable. Another personal example involves motions under Standing Order 43. I will not be called "Dr. No" any more.
You will not be called "Dr. Yes" either.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
1 think that the motions under Standing Order 43 have really become a charade. The whole rule of urgent and pressing necessity was rarely adhered to. The question of unanimous consent which is necessary to allow a motion to be put but not carried was something that I think many Members did not really understand. That was frequently displayed by the fact that when Members wished to speak on a motion under Standing Order 43 that had been allowed to be put, had received the unanimous consent, they would regularly stand up at the wrong time. This tells us that Members did not understand the process. If Hon. Members do not understand the process you can rest assured that the public does not understand it either. I believe it is a positive step to abandon that practice and proceed with this new system where we have a daily period of 15 minutes which, in my view, acts as a safety valve to allow Members to stand up and sound off on matters of concern. Since we do not have to get into the business of consent for putting motions, I think it will help make this place more understandable.
There is, as well, the question of parliamentary Journals. There are some recommendations which suggest that the Order Papers should have an index. That is desirable. Mr. Speaker, have you ever tried to find something in Monday's Order Paper? It can be pretty difficult sometimes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You have to understand it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
That is right. I have worked hard at it. I have a pretty good grasp of it. I suggest that if we can improve those Journals to the point where they become readily comprehensible and understandable it will be of great help. Those are three examples from the recommendations of the report which will make this place more understandable and practical.
Finally, I believe the members of this committee have a positive attitude which is spilling over into the entire House. That is a good effect. This positive attitude means that this experiment will quite likely work.

November 29, 1982
Parliamentary Reform
I suggest that this is a balanced report. It is interesting to note the eagerness with which members of the committee are looking to the remainder of their work. They are anxious to get their teeth into questions such as a review of the Estimates and into major Constitutional issues, such as what constitutes a motion of confidence. Hon. Members are enthusiastic about these subjects and they have built a head of steam in a positive way because they are approaching it from the viewpoint of parliamentarians instead of Opposition or Government Members.
I think that the mood of Hon. Members is healthy. Ironically, this mood is probably in direct contrast to what the public perceives the mood to be. I suggest that the public believes that we fight like cats and dogs in Parliament constantly. If they understood what has been happening on this committee I think they would applaud, welcome it and ask for more of this kind of co-operation. This co-operation has been brought about by many Members making a genuine attempt to make this place better. I think that we will succeed because Members want to make the House work better and they are approaching this change with that parliamentary attitude.
I believe that we will accomplish a great deal next year by proving that notwithstanding the fact that we may have very fierce partisan differences and notwithstanding that the struggle to form the Government will continue, that struggle will continue in a form that is more efficient and one in which the public interests are better served. As a result, I think this country will be better served in the long run.

Mr. Speaker, I feel somewhat out of my depth in speaking on this matter. It is the first time that I have ever spoken about the rules of this place. I do not apologize for that because the first thing I learned when I became involved in activities, which were admittedly somewhat more physical than politics, was what my coach told me: "Never mind the rules. If you do not know them, the referee will always give you a break." I have worked on that assumption and have functioned quite well here.
I realize that the motion which is before us today involves taking a step toward what I think are necessary changes, even for those of us who make no pretense of knowing the rules and thereby rely on the smarter Members to direct us. I do believe, however, like the Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) and the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), that there are certain things which we should keep in mind.
What we are witnessing today, in my crude analogy, is a group of undertakers preparing the body for burial. Everyone is praising everyone else. I see the jacket put on the deceased. I see the tie being tied. I see the rose put in the lapel and the cheeks being rouged. Everything is being done so nicely that all I can say is, heaven help us all if we do not get down and grapple with some of the real issues about the rules of this Parliament.
With respect to rule changes, everyone of those suggestions made during the experimental period, should be considered as
a small step forward. However, these changes are only cosmetic, unless, as several Members have indicated, the feeling of trust which seems to be surrounding this committee is maintained and supported by those who actually carry out the rules.
For instance, it means nothing whether speeches are 40 minutes or 20 minutes in length. If we want a more effective way to have shorter speeches, I suggest that we will not achieve it by artificially controlling the time. We only have to follow the rules that exist now, and simply insist that the speaker apply what the rules say, that a Member of the House shall not read his speeches. It is as simple as that. We would cut out 90 per cent of the oleaginous type of remark that politicians are wont to make. I am not suggesting that it will work, but perhaps it is a rule we might return to. We can simply return to the old-fashioned principle that if someone has something to say they do not have to read it. A Member may have two or three words written on a piece of paper, but if he speaks his mind, even if poorly expressed, we will understand him. When we allow many Members to read their speeches, it only deadens the whole debate. We cannot have a true debate when we hear a series of prepared speeches.
I am interested in the cosmetic techniques, as I call them, which were advanced that would allow Members to speak for only 20 minutes, with 10 minutes left for questions and answers at the end of their speeches. It will be interesting to see if those Members who have read their speeches can answer the questions. It may be a very wise experiment to see what happens to those Members who think they can appear knowledgeable by reading a written speech. They will be on their own when they are questioned on their remarks.
I am suggesting that the committee, which has assured us in the House today that it has achieved a consensus, a complete unanimity of trust amongst its members, will seriously consider the paper prepared by Hon. Members from eachside of the House, the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) and the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington). I have read that paper and I wholeheartedly agree that the heart and depth of what we must do is to give back to Parliament what it once had before 1968. We must do more, as well.
Whether we like it or not, there are many Hon. Members in the House, and there will be many more in a few years. I would like to think that one of the quickest ways to facilitate the functioning of the House is to give Hon. Members every opportunity to speak. The committee should give very serious consideration to what I call the Manitoba system, and I had nothing to do with developing it. At one time there was an NDP Government in Manitoba and a Conservative Opposition, and there was continual fighting in the Legislature. One Member from each side, a fairly senior Member and one who had been a federal Minister, got together and said, "Let us make this thing work and give the Government the chance to legislate and govern, but let us give the Opposition the chance to speak as well". They set up a system where the Legislature was meeting and, simultaneously, in another room, like in our
November 29, 1982

Railway Committee Room, another meeting was being held. If we had such a system, we could wander back and forth between two meetings so we could be in attendance at both places and have more opportunities to speak. There would be a little more freedom concerning the rules in speaking in the other place, which would usually be a committee of a very important sort.
This system introduced in Manitoba ten years ago has brought relative peace and harmony, and there has been very constructive work in that Legislature. 1 think we should call these two men as witnesses to our committee. They are both practical politicians, and I do not believe either of them is a lawyer. They could present their practical experience to our committee, and perhaps we could keep quite a few of our Members busy here and in another place at the same time, yet they would be free to come back and take part in votes and various functions. I put that proposition forth without saying anything more about it.
The second proposal is a longstanding one. To take care of the worry of the Conservative House Leader, the Hon. Member for Yukon, and it is legitimate, we must adopt the principle, on certain important matters, of setting up standing committees as statutory committees as opposed to the procedure carried out now whereby the Government decides to set up a committee and decides when the meetings are to be held, and so on. It should be put into statute. It would be preferable if the head of the committee were always a member of the Opposition and, second, if it had its own staff and were paid any sum of money to get the very best results. Such committees could do the job they are supposed to do but cannot do under our present system no matter how the amount of available time or number of speeches are juggled.
I do not know what the final choices will be concerning statutory committees, but I would suggest, first, that Public Accounts look at the expenditure of moneys. Second, before we spend the money Estimates should be prepared, which would put an end to the farce that we have been living under for the last 14 years in Estimates. Third, transportation should be considered. Two or three years ago a motion was presented by the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) concerning transportation safety and related matters. These matters should be dealt with by a statutory committee which is always sitting, which is free to call witnesses, and which has sufficient staff to handle this very difficult situation. For instance, I do not think there is a single person in Canada who can cope with railway accounting. We are always seeing ridiculous episodes where the railway says it is losing money and it is always disobeying the laws of Parliament, but we do nothing about that.
The situation became so bad some years ago that all Parties in Parliament agreed that the Department of Transport was not competent to handle railways, airlines or any transportation-related matters. We set up a giant Canadian Transport Commission and gave it all the powers of Parliament, putting it into statutory form. What was the result? The CTC was just ignored by the Government. Under the laws of this land, only Parliament could change the rates on the railways, yet it was
Parliamentary Reform
turned over to a man who wandered up and down, getting agreement from certain groups that the rates should be changed without the participation of Parliament. I refer to VIA Rail. Only the Canadian Transport Commission, under statute, has power to deal with something like VIA Rail, yet we had a Minister who simply ignored the CTC.
Parliament sits here, helpless. Until we can get these matters before a statutory committee which has power, not only to decide the facts, but also to take action on them, then all that we are discussing, designed to give us a chance to work together, is nothing but a sham or cosmetics.
From the temper of the speech of the Hon. Member for Yukon, I get the feeling that God help us all in the House if this committee does not come through with something substantive this year. All sorts of controversial matters have been listed, and we are told that this is what will be done in this year of grace. Many people will be interested to hear what will happen to several of the institutions here. We must trust that this committee will seize these matters and come to some conclusion, even though they are very sensitive matters.
I will refer back to the five statutory committees, and there may be others. There cannot be too many. It might not be possible to put others into special statutory form for several years, but I would suggest that those five would be a good start. I have listed Public Accounts, Estimates and Transportation, and the fourth and fifth are Statutory Instruments and Crown Corporations.
I want to end the second part of my conclusions. The Statutory Instruments Committee simply considers all our regulations. In many cases, not in the hundreds but rather in the thousands, evidence has come forward that the Civil Service has made regulations which have never been passed by Parliament. This is done through a certain little technique, and not a thing is done about it in this Parliament even though we have known about such occurrences for years. To everyone's disgrace in this Chamber, hardly anything has been done by us, with the exception of two or three of us, to protest this action. Let me give a couple of examples.
With reference to the power given to National Revenue, Parliament says that there will be no more succession duties, but regulations come through. A person dies and all of that person's property is deemed to have been sold at the date of death, and succession duties are collected without any approval of Parliament. For eight years I have tried to help orphans. The Minister has admitted, and Parliament says, that all orphans should receive family allowance, but the regulations state that orphans are not to receive it. The same applies to teenaged girls who become pregnant. These things make me annoyed.
I am staying here and I intend to win this battle, this war. Sooner or later, Parliament must back me up. There is no use in any of us coming down here, believing in certain things, if we know our rights, but not being able to do anything about them because of procedures. To the Minister's embarrassment, she stood up and said, "I cannot do anything about it, even

November 29, 1982
Parliamentary Reform
though 1 have admitted it". My request is, please, God, ensure that these people do their job and consider some items of substance under these rule changes next year.
There are many ideas in the Eluntington-Lachance report and many more ideas will be coming forward, I am sure. This trust that has developed in the committee, which is what the success of this report is based on, will it be maintained during this year and will it stand up to the serious changes that have to be made, the simple but serious changes to our rules? If they come through, they will have made their mark and served this country well.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to extend my congratulations to the members of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure. They worked for long hours all during the summer; they also worked wisely and productively, which is perhaps more important.
1 think they were very wise in recommending to us a package. I was here in the thirtieth Parliament when previous attempts to modernize our rules failed and they failed for a number of reasons, among them the fact that Members tried to improve on a little here and a little there, and the result was that there was no agreement.
The committee members clearly profited from this experience. They recommended a package, and they have asked all Parties to deal with the package as a whole.
The committee should also be congratulated on having brought in an unanimous report. Some of the best moments in this House and in committees happen when Members put aside partisan differences to work constructively on a project together. Putting aside differences does not mean failing to respect them or failing to take into account the realities of our democratic process, but it means working for compromise and consensus in a way that is as fair and as effective as possible. Those are some of the best moments, but they are rare moments.
The system seems to have put a premium on fireworks and on aggressive behaviour rather than on thoughtful, careful examination of issues. As a result, Members with more taste and talent for negotiation and compromise than for confrontation find the House a less satisfactory place to work than caucus or committees or other fields of endeavour.
Because I had a committee meeting this afternoon I was not able to hear all of the speech by the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker). If I understood him correctly in the brief excerpts that I did hear, he was saying that perhaps it is frustration with the system that leads Members to be less than constructive and that if offered a better and more satisfactory way of operating, Members would be glad to take it. I think he is right; and I think we have here a very useful beginning.
The committee members reminded us in their report that the purpose of parliamentary procedure is to enable a democratic assembly to operate effectively and fairly. The recommendations should lead to a much more effective use of time and more opportunity for knowledgeable, conscientious Members to participate publicly.
Members of Parliament on the Government side sometimes find that they may have influenced the development of a policy, but may not even speak in the debate in the House either because of the conflicting demands of committees or because they are very conscious of the need to get the legislation through. They feel that if there are going to be many long speeches from the Opposition they should keep their interventions to the absolute essential, so as not to delay the vote. But our constituents should not have to take it on trust that we are working for them. They should be able to see in the House some public evidence of what they hope and trust we are doing privately.
Some of the proposed recommendations that I think will be particularly helpful to all of us, on all sides of the House, include the recommendation that committees would be free to meet in the evening but that the House would rise at 6.30. This removes one source of time conflict, that is a committee sitting while there is a debate in the House that one would like to hear or participate in.
The second is the question of the parliamentary calendar. The proposal of fixed sittings, and particularly the committee's suggestion that the Government prepare a legislative program before each semester, certainly allows Members an opportunity for orderly planning and preparation. I hope that is an opportunity that will be well used.
Shorter speeches are clearly an advantage, but, as the Hon. Member who has just spoken has pointed out, a shorter speech in itself is not the answer. What is particularly useful, I think, is the proposal for a ten minute question and answer period at the end of each speech. That will certainly put an end to the practice indulged in by only a minority of Members of reading speeches prepared by their researchers but, more important, it will encourage us to listen to each other's speeches and it will provide an opportunity for questions that do advance the argument. Hopefully, knowing that there is that ten minute opportunity we will see fewer of the spurious points of order that are sometimes interjected now by people wanting to get in on the debate, but who are prevented from doing so. The suggestion that is also in this report that the interventions in that ten minute period be relevant and add a constructive element is perhaps an interesting suggestion for the speakers, and one that we hope will be acted on.
1 think we will all be glad to see the end of Standing Order 43 which has ceased to serve any useful purpose and is certainly not understood by the public. The proposal instead to allow Members to make statements for one and one half minutes on matters that they do wish to draw to the attention of the House seems a much better replacement for it.
The report gives a lot of attention to the role of standing committees, and all of these recommendations can only help,

that is, the smaller numbers and fewer substitutions, which should add very much to the quality of committee work, and the fact that committees will have the power to initiate inquiries. I am also pleased that the committee is recommending the continuance of special committees and task forces. These short, sharp task-oriented committees have proved their value in the last two years.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the committee recommended that examination of this procedure be ongoing. I think we can all agree that it is important to keep it contemporary and relevant. We have been given a very useful package here and I think it is important to give it full and fair trial for a year, as proposed.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy tonight to be able to speak for a few moments on what I believe to be a historic movement taking place in the House of Commons. I am happy also from the historic point of view to be in a discussion following almost immediately after the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), who spoke quite eloquently a few moments ago. He happened to be the first person I met who was a politician. Actually, he was a candidate. That was at the end of the Second World War when I was a high school student in Rosetown, Saskatchewan, and he had been brought back from Burma where he had been a pilot in the Air Force. I remember his campaign was quite different from those of today. I think he actually campaigned from an old J-3 Piper Cub and long-range on the rural telephone line. It is an interesting factor that the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain has been in this House for many years since and he is also speaking tonight on the question of renewal of the House. I believe what is really taking place is the first solid, concrete step in a renewal which I hope will be for the good, not only of this House of Commons, but for all of Canada. I would also like to join with the other Hon. Members from all Parties in congratulating the members of that committee which prepared the study which we are going to use as a trial effort in the House of Commons next year. The NDP House Leader, the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), is going around today with a very happy smile on his face. Probably the Hon. Members on both sides believe the smile indicates that he is only happy with this legislation before the House, but I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, the House Leader for the New Democrats has become a grandfather today for the first time, so he is taking on a sort of other aura of zeal, or whatever happens when you become a grandfather for the first time, and I would like to pay tribute to him and to his daughter, and particularly to his granddaughter, Melissa Folino, on her first day of life in Hamilton. I hope she lives to see this House of Commons become a much more effective place to operate.
Hear, hear!

The particular reason why I believe the legislation is so important tonight, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that I believe the House of Commons may find, through this new legislation, this new practice, a higher level and degree of credibility,
Parliamentary Reform
because I think the Members of this House have experienced with Canadians a frustration. Because they are Members of the House they are challenged over and over again by people who ask them what they are doing here. "Why do you act like that? Why are you not serious?" Again, as 1 have said in other speeches in this House, I have not met a single Member of Parliament who I feel is not serious. People do not come here unless they are serious, unless they really have the good of Canada at heart. I hope that through these steps that are being taken today under this motion everyone will benefit, and 1 thank those who have done the hard work over the past summer in bringing it about. I do hope the final result will be that there will be a new image of credibility arising from ail of us who are Members of this House of Commons.
Basically, the problem is that it is very difficult to have a large group of people do anything properly. My experience has been that if you put enough people together to do something, they will always do it poorly. That is not to say they are not trying. It is just simply difficult to have any large group of people do anything at the same time and do it well. Because we are all human beings, we do not do things perfectly.
This reform which we are working at now will not be the last reform. It is only a step. We will find it is imperfect, and something else will be needed down the road. However, the step is the important part, and that is why I rejoice with other Members in the House today who are so willing to accept this new effort. I am sure this motion will bring about progress and through it we will find a way in which the wisdom, knowledge and experience of the members who are here now, the future Members of the House of Commons and future Canadians, will be refined and directed in such a way that it can truly be a directive for the good of our country and for the good of the world, because we are part and parcel of the family of nations.
What I would like to speak on particularly is the length of the speeches. I feel that the short speech will be a much more effective speech. Anyone who has ever preached a sermon will know it is very easy to preach a long sermon and very difficult to preach a short one. The simple fact is that if we are going to say something concisely, it is necessary to work much harder preparing it. For that reason, 1 believe that speeches limited now to 20 minutes in the House, with the debate period afterwards in which the speaker can be challenged on his facts or presentation, will make for better speeches. I do not have any doubt about that at all and I am looking forward to it.
In the same light I would like to think that perhaps other modes of debate could be found which the committee can study. For instance, in the Congress of Brazil, which I am partly familiar with, the speaker speaks from the front. He speaks down toward the people in the House of Commons, which is a much easier way to speak. But at the same time there is another person from the Opposition who stands there also with a microphone, and the Speaker of the House can interrupt the debate at anytime to let the other person make his point. It turns into a real debate in which a point is made, which can be challenged by the other side. This is something

Parliamentary Reform
that could be looked at by the committee because there just has to be a better way to engage in debate than the way we do now.
I would also like to speak about the size of the committees. I really believe that bringing these committees down to a smaller size will be for the betterment of all. One of the best experiences I have had in the House of Commons was working on the North-South Task Force. I think the members of that task force, and other task forces that worked last year, will all relate a similar kind of experience. Working with a small group on a specific project, there was a kind of a friendship that grew between all three Parties. There was respect. The task force members were not changed, the attitude was, you were responsible, you were there and you did it. Therefore, I am happy to see we are going to try seriously to work with smaller committees, which I feel will do a lot more good down the road.
Something else I would like to speak about is the system of voting, and I hope the committee, as it continues its studies, will look at that problem. I call it a problem because so much time, to my mind, is wasted in the House waiting for the vote. As all Members of Parliament know, when the bell rings there is a kind of great vacuum which starts in the life of a Member of Parliament while he waits for the vote. That can be 15 minutes or 16 days. You just do not know when the vote is coming. Last week we had a vote here which was called at about six o'clock. The vote was finally taken at 7.15 in the evening. For that hour and 15 minutes I felt really frustrated, along with everyone else in this House. I really believe that has to change. I would suggest that the Committee look at modern voting techniques like that which is used at the United Nations. It is an electronic voting device, with buttons on the desk with which the Member can indicate his vote. There are buttons for yes, no, abstain and absent. That is all you can do with this kind of a voting system. It should be possible to have an electronic voting system. We could keep the traditional vote for six or seven times a year to make sure that Hon. Members could stand up and be counted. That has some reason to it. But not for all the votes. If some of the votes could be, let us say, on a 30-minute bell, or the vote would be scheduled for eight o'clock, I say that it should be possible for a Members of Parliament to vote anytime prior to that, and it should be done electronically. It could be done in any part of the House of Commons, Confederation Building, West Block, wherever. If we each were issued a card which had an electronic code on it, we could put in a slot some place and our vote would be recorded. At 7.30 or eight o'clock the Speaker could indicate the vote was counted and the results would be listed on a board. The count would be there and the press or anyone else could print it in the newspaper the next morning. I think people might be more interested if they had a vote count everyday.
They'd think they were at a hockey game.

No, they would not. They would have a feeling they knew what was going on. I do not know how many people in Canada know when we vote or what the votes are, but I think that kind of system would make it much easier for all the people of Canada to know how their Member voted. They would know whether he or she were there, yes, no, or whatever, it could be reported and printed in the paper every day after a vote.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that what is happening today is a good thing but it is just the beginning. We have not done many of the things that could be done. I think the life of an MP, having talked to some of the older Members, is more difficult today because of the speed of a lot of things, transport being one. Members go home to their ridings every Friday night, like myself, spending six or seven hours on the plane each way. In the old days Members came down in September on the train, a nice slow ride down, stayed in Ottawa till Christmas, when they might go back. It was very different then. Interestingly enough-and all the Members can speak to this-everyone finds one or two or three constituents on the plane every trip we make. It is a great place to get information, but the work keeps on because the constituent finally has his or her Member belted down. You cannot get up, they will tell you exactly what they want you to hear. It is great.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have had the chance to say a few words on this motion tonight. I do not see a great light shining yet, but there is a little glimmer down at the end of the tunnel, and I believe with this step and others which will come, the knowledge, experience and wisdom of the people in this House will be directed more clearly and exactly in the direction Canadians want it to be directed.

Credit for that should go of course to our chairman, the Hon. Member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre), and the two Vice-Chairmen, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans). But I would be remiss in not mentioning the work done over the years by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), a man who has served this institution well for nearly 40 years, and for whom many of us have the greatest respect, and in whom many of us see the repository of every procedural wisdom. This report is only the beginning, Mr. Speaker. In a sense we have just tinkered with the rules, but in such a way as to mark a beginning in the real reform of this House. Let us focus on three things: the parliamentary calendar, which is going to make it more rational for the Government to get its program through Parliament; the parliamentary timetable, which will have the effect of making the House a more humane environment in which to work; then there is the enhancement of the MPs role. So this report is only the beginning. Some may say it is too modest, but it took a lot of discussion and soul-searching. After the report was tabled it took a lot of soul-searching on the part of the Parties to accept it. In particular I would like to pay tribute to our House Leader, who has just come into the House, for having facilitated the easy passage of this report through the Government. I believe that was no mean feat, because there were reservations on the Government side, as I am sure there were reservations in the other two Parties. But the fact is that the Government and the Opposition have shown their faith in the members of the committee. That in itself is a significant fact. It is significant for those of us who have participated in that committee.
Where do we go from here? The Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) made an excellent point. There is some responsibility with the Chair, Mr. Speaker, and 1 am speaking to you and your colleagues in the chair directly. There are some things we cannot do in changing the rules. We can only have faith in you and your colleagues that you will apply the rules in the best spirit. The point made by the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain was indeed a very salient one, that the rules in effect now should be enforced. I am talking about the rules of relevance and the basic courtesies of the House in the Standing Orders, which should be observed and enforced by the Chair. I hope this debate will in a sense make you, Mr. Speaker, feel obligated to deal with this matter very seriously.
The thing I want to dwell upon, Mr. Speaker, is the third point I raised, the enhancement of the role of the backbenchers. In the last 25 years the Government has come to dominate the House. Indeed, it is in the last 100 years, both here and at Westminster. This cannot be helped because society has become more complex, the demands on Government more stringent; but the power of the executive must be checked, not only for the sake of the country and the institution but for the sake of the government itself. A hundred years ago, Mr. Speaker, in Westminster and in this House most of the legislation which came forward was private Members' Bills. Now, most of the time it is government time. Private Members' time is relegated to three hours a week. I would hope in our next round of discussion in the Committee that we will look seriously at bringing private Members' motions and Bills to fruition so that there is division on these questions, so that a private Member can regularly have the opportunity of saying "I brought this piece of legislation to the House and I had it accepted by my colleagues." Let us not be so naive as to think the only repositories of wisdom in Parliament reside on the Treasury benches, with all respect.

Hear, hear!

Spending power must be brought under more effective control. My colleagues, the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) and the Hon. Member for Rose-mont (Mr. Lachance) have brought forward a report which warrants detailed scrutiny and which is being looked at by the Committee right now.
The rule of the Whip should be examined. I see my good friend, the chief Government Whip here, and I would say to him, through you, Mr. Speaker, that this will be the last Parliament where any Government is able to enforce the Whips no matter what. The nature of Canadian society is changing and Parliament is changing, as evidenced by this committee's report, and government must change. 1 am heartened because the Government has accepted this report and it will take the lead from members of the committee.
Hear, hear!

But there are times when a backbencher may wish to break ranks with his side. There must of course be matters of absolute confidence. We must ensure that any move to a Congressional style system is not allowed to go too far- some people want more of a Congressional system here, and we are getting that with the innovations in the committee system which are being accepted-and we have to be very careful that the very notion of responsible government in the parliamentary context, where the government gets it power from the House of Commons, is not diminished. We must make sure that the spending power, the Royal prerogative, rests with the executive. We as backbenchers can demand more power but we cannot usurp the basic responsibility of the government to initiate spending and taxing legislation. If we do, we are undermining the whole system of British parliamentary democracy.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, I suppose I should say that my concept of the role of a Member of Parliament is that 1 have an obligation to my Party. There is no doubt that I would not be standing here today if it were not for my Party. I have an obligation to my constituents-not only those who voted for me, but all of them. I must serve all of them once I am elected, no matter who voted for me.
I have an obligation to my conscience. Members of this House who sat in the Thirtieth Parliament had to look to their consciences on the subject of capital punishment. There was a lot of pressure, both inside the House and outside. We have to answer to our own consciences. All Members have an obligation to their conscience.
Those obligations mean nothing to the final obligation which, I submit, is that every Member of this House has the obligation to the institution of Parliament. If the institution of Parliament, as it has developed in the last 800 years in Great Britain and in this country, is diminished in any way, then the very foundations of democracy will be weakened.

Parliamentary Reform
We are but an island in a sea of tyranny in the latter part of the twentieth century. The reason we are that island of sanity in a sea of tyranny is because of the parliamentary system and because this committee has come forward with a report which will be accepted by the House. To me, that means that the parliamentary system is alive and well. At a moment when people were writing it off as being irrelevant, at a moment when Canadians were questioning the value of their institution, we have shown that Parliament can still work, that there is a way to go, that there is a future for this institution.
With my colleagues, I look forward to the resumption of our work in this session and in the new session. Within the next year we hope to bring a new meaning to the words "parliamentary democracy."

Mr. Speaker, I followed with a great deal of interest the comments of the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Collenette) as he made his trip to Damascus. He has seen the light. I cannot help but wonder how it is that the Government came to the point where it was prepared to bring together Members from all sides of the House to examine the position to which the House had been brought by the Government and its method of governing and to come forward with a report, even as helpful as this one is.
The Hon. Member for York East mentioned our obligation to this House. I do not deny that obligation. But we also have an obligation to Canada, Mr. Speaker.
When we decided to put ourselves up for election and seek the support of Canadians it was because we believed there was something fundamentally wrong with the way the country was being governed, and perhaps with the institutions through which it was being governed.
I take full cognizance of the admonition of the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) that we must not just pat one another on the back about this; we must bring to it a critical eye. We should bring to this a fair amount of skepticism, because of the manner in which the Government has handled the country's business.
I ask myself why the Government agreed that the committee should meet. For three or four years there have been opportunities for the Standing Committee on Procedures and Organization to meet, but the Government has not responded to demands for meetings, so I approach the whole issue with a healthy skepticism. Aside from that, Mr. Speaker, my comments this evening will be confined to two or three areas.
One area relates to committees. This is dealt with in Section (5) on page 18 of the report of the Special Committee on Standing Orders on Procedures, Issue No. 7. This deals with Committees in a variety of ways. In certain cases the size of the committee has presented difficulty, but this problem has been settled. I think we should be prepared to accept the figures that are given. There may have to be exceptions in one or two committees, as has been the case with the Standing Committee on Agriculture and the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. It may be that the latter will have to be divided into two committees. That
possibility has not been mentioned but it should not be excluded from the committee's review.
Substitutions within a committee is another matter that concerns me. I am glad we are not being inflexible about membership of this committee or that. When an issue arises which is of prime concern to a particular Member at a particular time and is coming up in another committee, that Member should have the opportunity to find a place on that committee, on 24 hours' notice. In that way the Member can represent the views of constituents much more easily than can be done in the House or, if the Member has certain expertise, it can be made available to the committee. I think there has been an attempt to remove inflexibility, and the 24 hours' notice required is a good move.
To my way of thinking the provision for automatic referral of annual reports and other reports to committees, will make the committee system work. It has not worked in the past, Mr. Speaker.
There are a couple of other matters dealt with in Subsections (c) and (d) on page 19 of the report which deserve comment and study, which I hope they will receive in the Committee. The automatic referral of the annual reports of Departments, Crown corporations and their subsidiaries and other agencies to the appropriate standing committee immediately after they are tabled in the House, is important. Even more important is that such tabling should initiate sessions of that committee. There is no reference whatsoever to having the committees meet to consider the reports. That is an oversight which I hope will be corrected.
I am certain that this report is going to be accepted, and I am glad to see that there will be a continuing review of the Standing Orders. I hope that all recommendations that cannot be put into the Standing Orders in the years ahead can be reviewed, and if approved in committee can immediately be instituted with the procedures of the committee. One way of achieving that would be that any five Members of the committee could go to the Chairman with a request to meet to discuss the matter in committee and to report within a week. There should be an opportunity for Members to take that action. It could be five members representing two Parties. There are instances today of very, very important issues that do not receive study because the Fisheries Committee cannot meet on two matters. There is a report of the Fisheries Committee on the West Coast and a report of the Fisheries Committee on the East Coast. We have tried to bring a meeting about in the House, we have tried behind the curtains and we have tried with the Minister, but he says it is not his business and he cannot order the committees to meet.
There should be provision in the regulations to permit any committee that has a report in front of it, to meet in order to consider that report, or even to write its own terms of reference. It has to be an agreed reference so that the four or five Members, or however many it needs, can insist that the meeting take place within two days. So much for the automatic referral. This is a shortcoming in Section (5)(c).

Turning to the Government response to committee reports, I notice that the Elouse Leader on our side commented about it earlier. He said that it shall be at the request of the committee that the Government table a comprehensive response. Frankly, that is not good enough. I think the Government should be required under the Standing Orders to reply to every recommendation that any committee makes. If the committees are to have any meaning whatever, the Government must respond to their recommendations. If they do not make any recommendations, it is unfortunate and perhaps the committees are falling down on the job. But if they do make recommendations, each one should have a response from the Government, yes or no. There may be questions of policy, money or ideology which would prevent the Government from adopting this or that recommendation, but it should be required to say so within a certain length of time, be it 120 days or six months.
I believe that item by item, recommendation by recommendation, the Government should be required to reply to the reports of committees, whether they be departmental reports, reports on Crown corporations, their subsidiaries or other agencies. I think this is vital, to give those who sit on committees the feeling that they are getting some feedback from the Government for the work they have done.
Another matter on which I think it is worth commenting is Private Members' Business. There is no provision for Private Members' Business to be voted on, except when there is no quorum. Apparently that can be done in the House in those circumstances, for which we should all be ashamed. In the normal course of business there must be some provision in Section (6) so that there is an opportunity for a Private Member's Bill to be brought to a vote, either for the subject matter to be referred to committee or for it to be rejected. Otherwise, it is just a matter of having an hour of debate as provided here and it goes to the bottom of the list, which is 438 or whatever, and there is no vote. I believe we should have a provision in here for a vote. I see that the provision in the Standing Orders has to be rewritten. It indicates that the proceedings on any Bill or motion in the name of a private Member shall be interrupted one hour after being taken up and considered. That is just an airing of an idea. Surely there is a means, even on a Wednesday afternoon, of having a vote on a matter which is in a private Member's Bill.
Section (7) of this particular report deals with a continuing review of the Standing Orders. If I understand correctly, the committee will more or less be in permanent session. I hope to call on a number of Members of the Committee to examine and obtain reports on how various recommendations are working out in the House and to be able to modify them in the course of the year. I hope this is not a document written in stone for 12 months. If, as I suggested, there could be agreement on the requirement to have a vote on a private Member's Bill or to have the Government reply item by item or recommendation by recommendation to reports of committees, and if the committees could agree on those matters, I hope it could be brought back to the House between December 21 this year and
Parliamentary Reform
December 21 next year and instituted in our order of proceedings. I think we could probably manage to live with that sort of thing.
It was never quite clear in my mind, except that we were coming to the end of the calendar year and the requirement to have a debate, why the committee brought its work to an end at this particular stage of the proceedings. I am not sure why other matters were not considered and brought forward. Therefore, I feel that a continuing review of the Standing Orders by the committee should be of a nature to permit it to come to the House with modifications based upon experience.
Another matter which is not clear in my mind is what will happen on December 21, 1983. This has been referred to as a package deal. It is an all or none proposition. What will happen on December 21, 1983? Do we have to buy all that is here, all that has been modified during the year, or will there be a seriatim vote on elements which have improved the House of Commons and a rejection of elements which have proven themselves to be unworthy of the House of Commons? I hope it is a matter the committee will consider, that if we are not committed to this package there will be no package at all. Some of it is experimental, we agree. I hope it will go on for a year, but do we have to buy the whole report as it stands?

Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate this evening.

I have been a member of the committee. Although my name does not appear on the list of members in the report, I am still a member of the committee. I recognize that I have not attended all the meetings, but this was because they conflicted with my duties and obligations to the Standing Committee on Transport.
This has been one of the finest debates I have heard in the House since coming here. Until just a few minutes ago, it was a debate which one could term to be all sweetness and light. The Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) seems to have some grave misgivings about the report, and I should like to take a minute to answer a couple of his concerns.
