Parliamentary Reform
I associate myself with all the remarks which have been of a congratulatory nature to the Chairman and the two ViceChairman of the committee. 1 have a great deal more confidence in the ability of the House to act, as a result of having served on the committee and having seen all its members work in close harmony. Very often the most strenuous arguments were among Members of the same Party rather than among Members of different Parties. I think this is very good for the future of this institution.
Because of a reference from the Government a few months ago, I had the privilege of dealing with the domestic air carrier policy in the Standing Committee on Transport. We had the same experience then in the Standing Committee on Transport as we had in this committee on procedure reform. It seems to me that is a time when Members of Parliament are, in fact, serving the interests forwhich our constituents sent us here, when we are being Members, not only for an electoral district but Members for the country as a whole, and when we are proposing policy or passing legislation that deals with the good of all Canadians and not just making representations for a particular area of the country. I want to deal very briefly with three areas.
First, I would like to say that there are four things that give me a great deal of encouragement. We unanimously presented a report that deals with the hours of sitting. Already I have heard some concern expressed about what Members are going to do with their evenings. 1 do not have that concern and I do not believe that it should be the role of a committee on standing orders and procedure to try to devise rules that will protect the morality or ethics of the Members of this House. Surely to God they established their ethical conduct before coming here. If they have not, it is something for their constituents to deal with and not a committee of this House.
The fixed timetable, to which other Members have spoken, is something that I think is of vital importance to all of us so that we can order our lives in such a manner as to be able to spend an appropriate amount of time in the capital of the country and yet have sufficient time to deal with our constituencies and with our families.
Third, I think the reform of the committee system is vitally important to the survival of this institution. I do not have the concerns expressed by the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich. I am not prepared, at this moment at least, to bring to the committee the idea that every report from a committee must be responded to by the Government. There are some reports from committees to which a response is not appropriate, Mr. Speaker. Surely it is within the wisdom of members of a particular committee to make the decision as to whether or not there should be a response to the Government. I think the wisdom of the committee in making that recommendation is a strength and not a weakness.
What of the future of the committee? There are many areas that have been dealt with today by other speakers, and I do not
want to be too repetitive but I do want to deal with three of those areas. The first is non-confidence votes.
It is very important that we change the manner in which we conduct non-confidence votes. This point was brought up first this afternoon by the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan). There is a good deal of wisdom in what he said. We must get away from this idea that every vote is a vote of confidence. Surely by now we can progress enough so that Members of Parliament on both sides of the Chair can make a determination as to whether or not a proposed piece of legislation is worthy of passage by this House without having the whips applied. I think we would have better legislation and more carefully thought out legislation and we would have a much better functioning House if there were not a vote of nonconfidence attached to the vote on every Bill. I believe it is absolutely essential that the regulations formulated under a Bill be brought back either to the House or to an appropriate committee of the House for study because many things can be done by regulation, as the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) pointed out, that were not intended to be done by the House when it passed the legislation. That should come under the scrutiny of Parliament, just as the enabling legislation does. I hope the committee will deal with that point. If we 5566;-1 deal with that, we will provide backbenchers with much more freedom of action and with more adequate representation, not only of their constituents but of the country at large. We will have a much more vibrant and lively institution here. We will have a much greater sense of worth on the part of the individual backbencher that he will have some power and will be able to call the Government to account, that the Government must listen to the elected representative of the people and not just to the advisers of the Government and of the bureaucracy. That, to me, is of vital importance.
I hope from what I have heard here today that the expectations of this House for the work of the committee will not become too exalted. With all of the nice things that have been said about the committee today, it must be remembered that we are 20 members, none of whom are infallible, and we will not solve every problem of this House in the course of our deliberations. Not everything we do will be perfect. We will have to do some of it over. Mistakes will be made on the committee, and I think that should be accepted as a fact. We will not be able to come in with a perfect set of reforms. Reform is an ongoing procedure.
We do, indeed, have an obligation to this House, an Hon. Member said. I forget who it was, unfortunately. In my opinion, parliamentary democracy is probably the noblest institution of Government ever devised by mankind. It will only be noble as long as it is relevant. Those of us who serve in Parliament are finite mortal creatures who will wither and die. While we are here, if we do not work to revitalize this institution it, too, will become finite and mortal. It does not have to be so. It does not have to be a finite institution. It can be an institution with some immortality, with a great, long life, much longer than that of any human. It has already had a life much
November 29, 1982

longer than that of any human. We must make sure with these reforms that the Parliament of Canada remains a vibrant, lively institution that serves the needs of Canadians, not only for today and tomorrow, but for many future generations.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to rise and speak to the third report of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure. Hon. Members might expect, having served on the committee, that I am a bit biased in favour of the report. 1 must confess that is true.
This was a wise report, and I hope the future will show that to be so. The basis for my conclusion about it being wise is not simply because 1 am a member of the committee. Like other members, I try to reserve the right to say no, the right to say that I do not agree with something that is going on, whether within my own Party or within the Government. I believe other Members have approached the task in that same vein. Therefore, I believe the report does have a balance with which we can live.
I consider myself still to be a new Member in terms of Standing Orders, even though I was elected to this House in 1979. I suppose in many jobs after a few years you feel you have mastered it and it is time to move on. But I am just beginning to realize and to understand how this place works, its inadequacies and how it could be made to work better. I can remember during the first nine months being on the Government side the absolute frustration at what seemed to be pointless opposition from the Liberals then in Opposition. I can remember my anger at realizing in 1978 that the then minister of justice had brought in a budget and our Party in Opposition opposed it. That was its state in the 1979 elections. When we returned to the government side, we put those same budget proposals, as if we were supporting them, and the Liberal Opposition was opposing them. This continued for some time. The further absurdity happened when we were defeated in 1980 and not all of those finance provisions were put through. Here were the Liberals, back in the government, putting those same proposals forward and we opposed them. As a new Member of Parliament, that had to be the crowning irony for me as to how absurd things were here.
And there is no doubt that being elected does not mean one must become a eunuch or someone who becomes immediately dumb and can only stand or sit when the Party says. I certainly do not intend to give up my right to speak out, and I hope other Members do not give up that right either. There is no doubt that Parliament itself will be an adversary process. One of the recommendations of the committee report is to allow that debate, because there is no doubt that we are locked into a battle for the hearts and minds of Canadians. Government is the exercise of power, including the power to take away the lives of its citizens. That is how much power governments have. The Liberal Party on one side, the NDP and our Party
Parliamentary Reform
on the other side are locked into a battle for the hearts and minds of Canadians. We hope to win and they do as well.
The House will always be an adversarial place. Undoubtedly, there is no reason why the committees, the task forces and the special committees from which this report is a product, can become much less adversarial, because the purpose of these bodies is to group people around a problem. If they can address the problem and have experts express their views on it, a solution to the problem can be found, irrespective of the various philosophies in terms of the exercise of executive power and how the country should be run. With a little goodwill in these committees, free of the public television which exists in the House, surely we can come to a wiser result. That is what has happened in task forces, since 1980.
I had the privilege of being a member of the Committee of Fiscal Federalism. That committee got around the problem of how this nation should operate fiscally with the huge wealth and different views of its different regions. A report was issued from that committee which was also unanimous. While the Government did not accept all of the recommendations of the committee, several were adopted. Speaking for my own Province of Alberta with respect to that fiscal federalism report, the people of Alberta who I spoke to were very pleased with the parts of the report that reflected their view. I was thankful to the Members opposite and those in the NDP who agreed to including those views. I was able to return to my region, as a federal Member of Parliament, and say that Parliament is working for them, and I was able to produce the hard, cold facts.
I was pleased to be asked to serve on this Special Committee on the Standing Orders. Once again, the process was good. We argued about some subjects, shared a few drinks and had special meetings until those problems disappeared when we realized that we were facing a common problem.
One of those common problems was that which an elected Member faces with the power of the bureaucracy. There is no doubt that there has been an enormous growth in the bureaucracy federally, provincially and municipally since the Second World War. While individual civil servants are very fine people who work well within their jurisdictions, the Civil Service collectively has taken on a life of its own which is getting out of hand.
I believe that the same argument applies to Crown corporations. There is nothing inherently evil in the operation of a Crown corporation, but at the federal level where there are almost 600 Crown corporations and where there are almost as many at the provincial level across the country, there is no doubt that there is not enough fiscal control of that sub-level of Government.
I hope that we have taken steps to bring this under control as a result of our third report. However, I believe we must go even further in the future. Some Members have been concerned about the report. All that I can say to them is to let us try it. If it does not work we will change it. If that again does not work, we will change it again. If it is totally inadequate by

November 29, 1982
Parliamentary Reform
next December we can revert back to this antiquated procedure where we can have four or five changes of Government which will be proposing and opposing something in the same absurd way.
In the future our committee will deal with Supply. I think this will be a relief to many Members. We will deal with the role of the Speaker and with votes of confidence. As I have come to know Members opposite, and even a couple from the NDP, I have no doubt that we can come to an agreement.
The question of private Bills was a critical issue which we dealt with in the report. As you know, Mr. Speaker, we have so far received over 100 submissions from individuals and groups. Those people feel unquestionably that the role of the private Member of Parliament is important. Yet, when we look at our parliamentary timetable, we do not see much time for private Members' Bills to be handled. 1 believe that switching consideration of private Members' Bills to Wednesday is a very good idea. We have some other ideas which will make that process much more solid.
With no disrespect to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) 1 believe absolutely contrary to what he said about our being nobodies once we get 50 yards away from the Hill and being somebodies only on the Hill, I have found the opposite to be true. I find that I am nobody on the Hill because I am locked into a system where the bureaucracy has much more power. When I return to my riding, my constituents are pleased to see their Member of Parliament and speak with him. Therefore, 1 think that I am somebody when 1 am more than 50 yards away from the Hill, and I am not as important here.
I hope that Members will support the committee report so that we will have their critical analysis to make this a better place when future reports are tabled.

Mr. Speaker, I am also a member of the committee which has its interim report before the House tonight. I have had ample opportunity to state my views in committee, so I will just take a minimum of time in the House tonight. I understand that one of the two Vice-Chairmen, the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), intends to speak, and perhaps we can use the remaining 20 minutes.
I would first like to thank the House and the Government House Leader (Mr. Pinard) for the opportunity to be on this committee. It was an exciting undertaking and one of the more pleasant aspects of my parliamentary career which spans some nine years, counting the years spent in the Newfoundland House, which was better. At the outset I would also like to congratulate the Chairman of the Committee, the Hon. Member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre) and the two Vice-Chairmen, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain, as well as the members of the committee, for doing an excellent job to date.
I want to draw particular attention to the speed and dispatch with which the committee members, under the leadership of the Chairman and the two Vice-Chairmen, used in establishing a rather productive working relationship from the very outset.
The fact is that the work of this committee is not an indictment of this institution, of Parliament. This institution has survived over 700 years over some very difficult periods, periods which were so dramatic that, by comparison, the now famous bell-ringing incident just pales into insignificance. The institution has seen some rather dramatic periods and has survived them and been all the better for them. This committee is not in any way an indictment. Therefore, it is incorrect to question the validity of the institution. Rather, it is proof of the strength of this institution which has evolved over the years to the point at which it requires new rules to meet changing times. This is not the first time the rules of this institution have been changed and it will not be the last.
The interim report, as significant as it is in many respects, is really only the tip of the iceberg. As Hon. Members know, an iceberg is eight-ninths, or almost 90 per cent, below the surface, and so it is with the work of the committee. The real impact, the real substance, I suggest, lies ahead. The full impact has not yet surfaced.
There are other issues we want to address. They have already been mentioned by Hon. Members, such as the issue involving the MP and the bureaucracy, which I want to see the committee address, as I believe it will. The issue involving the several aspects of accountability is already receiving the attention of the committee and of a sub-committee, in particular, and the House has already heard about that today. The issue of the Speakership is one which we want to consider. The issue as to how we should vote in the Chamber, as to whether it is the most efficient method or, even more important, whether it is the right method for this particular time, is also one which I should like to see addressed and one which 1 know we will.
A few moments ago the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) raised a number of important questions about this experiment. He is not in the Chamber at the moment, but I am sure he will have the opportunity to hear my response to his questions so far as I am capable of responding.
I want to say in particular to him, and to the House, in case someone may not be aware, that the committee, of which I am a member and whose report we are considering right now, has no implementation function. Its mandate is to investigate and report. Therefore, one should avoid thinking of the committee as some kind of administrator or implementation structure which would sit in judgment of the actions of the House to decide just how well a rule is being implemented or if it suits or satisfies the intent of the committee. I submit that the committee's work is done once it has reported to the House and once it has made its recommendations, either on an interim or on a final basis, so that the real adjudicators of the experimental package are the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the Hon. Member for every other riding in the country. Only he and the other Hon. Members of the House can answer this question.
I am sure that over the experimental period of one year we will all come to some conclusions as to which items in the
November 29, 1982

package have improved the functioning of the House and which items we could well do without. 1 have no doubt, I say to him, that over the year we will find a consensus emerging about which parts of the package we ought to retain on a more permanent basis and which parts we ought to throw out before they do any further damage.
The same gentleman raised the question as to why the committee brought in an interim report at this particular time.
I want to say to him that there was no magic reason why it was done at this particular time, except to say that the committee found reasonably quickly that there were a number of items on which it was fairly easy to get a ready consensus. We decided that we would recommend them to the House as an experimental package. That is something of an oversimplification, but that is basically the answer to the question raised by the Hon. Member. We have come forward at this time because we have identified some items concerning which we foresaw the possibility of a consensus. We were apparently right, given the rather rapid fashion in which the three caucuses accepted the recommendations in the interim report.
The real spirit of the report was summed up a few minutes ago by the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker). He is also a member of the committee, and he said, "Let us try it". This is an experiment. None of us are particularly married to it. We naturally feel some favour toward it or we would not have come to the House and recommended it. We feel it has a reasonable chance of success. However, the only way we will know whether what we put on paper will work in practice is to give it a try. So, in the spirit of the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills and, I believe, of every Hon. Member in the House, let us try to see if it will work. I believe it will. If it needs some honing, refinement, so be it. In the meantime, while we try this package, 1 am rather encouraged that the committee work will continue in depth on some of the other issues I have mentioned. Other Hon. Members of the House and of the committee, in particular, have mentioned some. I would even suggest that there may well be an issue or two we have not really focused on yet, of which we have not seen the significance. Certainly, I have not, and I bow and defer to people On the committee who have been in the House much longer than I and who have been involved in other reform exercises such as this particular one. However, for my part, I have the distinct feeling or impression that we will come across a whole area that we have not addressed in any depth.
Therefore, I say, let us get on with the experiment. I believe that we have unanimity on this point, pretty well. I also say, let us get on with the larger task of the committee because if we are to measure, with any accuracy, the validity of having set up this committee in the first place, I ask Hon. Members not to measure it in terms of tonight's exercise but, rather, to wait and see what comes forward insofar as the larger issues are concerned, the issues to which we referred in our various speeches.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
D'accord!
Parliamentary Reform
This is really an historic night when my good friend, the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), and I are saying "Aye, aye" to the same point.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Never! You go too far!

It gives me reason to ask if we really do not have a good thing here. It is so good that he can accept it and I can accept it with absolute agreement. It is absolutely amazing.
I am glad to be associated with the report and I look forward as a member of the committee to continuing the work which has been so well begun. This work could not go forward without the very active collaboration and understanding of every Hon. Member of the House, and that is not a buttered up way of saying that people have been in agreement with everything we have done. There have been some volatile arguments on aspects of this report involving items that we are now considering. That is not the point I make. The point I make is that I feel, irrespective of Party lines, a willingness and almost an anxiety to find rules which will serve us and this institution better. It is that spirit which is making tonight's exercise possible. It is that spirit which gives me confidence that we will come up with an over-all report, a final report as a committee, which will serve this institution and the people of Canada very well.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to say a few words at the close of this debate on the motion of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) concerning the subject matter of the third report of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure. I, too, congratulate the movers of the motion and the members of the committee who brought us to this historic point in parliamentary life. As a ten-year Member and a three-year president of standing committees of the House, I welcome these changes and I want to comment on just a few of them.
The idea of planning on a semester basis will be an excellent discipline for both the Government and the Opposition. The Government will be forced to think a little further ahead than they now do, and the Opposition will be able to plan in a much more orderly fashion. They are now only able to learn the business of the House the week before it begins.
As far as the parliamentary calendar is concerned, and rising for the summer recess on the thirtieth of June, I note that the calendar will give us 175 sitting days a year instead of 165 days. I think that is good because, if it is needed, we should have that, knowing the ending date should end the brinksmanship that we see at practically every end of a session in the House now. The Government is always wanting to push through more things before the end, and the Opposition is always threatening to hold things up. Then there is a threat to make us sit longer. The idea of never knowing is very hard on the personal lives of Members, and very hard on the families of Members. Family life should be improved for all Members by the installation of this new calendar.

November 29, 1982
Parliamentary Reform
Previously, the summer recess coincided roughly with the academic school year. The children got out of school on the thirtieth and the MPs got out of the House on June 30 and they could all go to their ridings and their homes for the summer recess, and that was fine. In the last ten years only once, in 1978, did the House rise on June 30. In other years, excluding two years in which the House did not sit because of summer elections, the House rose in late July. I would just like to read out these dates, Mr. Speaker, July 27, July 30, July 14, July 25, July 23 and July 17, and this year, 1982 set the record when the House adjourned on August 4. I am sure we all remember that long, hot summer.
On the daily timetable aspect, I think that would be good for families as well. As I analyse the changes, I see that they really have only shifted the 8 to 10 p.m. sitting to 11 in the morning on Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the Adjournment Debate has been moved from 10 p.m. to 6 p.m. That debate is generally sparsely attended. I suppose the only effect of that is that it will keep a few Parliamentary Secretaries busy through part of the dinner hour. I said that this daily timetable was good for families as well. That is assuming that the Members take advantage of the close of debate at 6 and go home to their families, if they have them here. Other suggested uses of that evening time is other meetings, or travel, or study in your office or office work, et cetera. I think one or two Members may have alluded to it, but it may be the "et cetera" that will prove to be the problem. Long ago, I am told on good authority, night sittings were introduced for the very purpose of keeping Members of Parliament busy at night, and keeping them off the streets and out of the night spots and other dangerous places in the national capital region.
Speak for yourself.

I say that only half in jest, but on a very serious note I do hope that the evening time from 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. is not taken up immediately by extra committee meetings. My committee, the Public Accounts Committee, traditionally sits at 11 a.m., so if we continue to sit then we will miss the 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. period of the House. Furthermore, the benefits that might accrue to the Members will certainly be lost to the staff who have to service that committee, if they have to come back here and work until ten o'clock.
We have been considering the size of the committee in the Public Accounts Committee for some time. I judge from the report that we will be getting ten Members instead of the current 20. That is not a problem as some of you know who have attended Public Accounts Committee meetings in the last number of years. We have to make a special effort, in the Public Accounts Committee, to get a quorum for conducting votes in the committee because our quorum is 11 and our normal attendance is usually in the seven range. We will be better organized with having only ten. I do not know what the quorum will be, probably six. We will probably have at least six most of the time.
The limitation on substitution will also be good for most committees. As I analyse how it might apply to Public Accounts I can see that it will eliminate the very few occasions that we have had where a lot of Members have come in order to achieve some special end that the Government might have wanted to achieve in one of those meetings. I think it might also prevent substitution of so-called experts, in subjects which the members of Public Accounts Committee are not expert. When these Members come in, although they are expert on their subjects, they are not experts on the proceedings and methods of the Public Accounts Committee. We very often find that their visit, while pleasant, has not been as useful to the committee as we all thought it would be.
One very important aspect of the committee's recommendations, Mr. Speaker, is the response to Committee reports. I suppose the Public Accounts Committee makes more reports to the House of Commons than any other. We get no official response from the House on these reports. The President of the Treasury Board usually replies, at least the last one did-I am not sure as I have not filed a report since the new one was named. He always replied to our reports by letter to let us know whether the Government agreed or did not agree. Again, in my memory, only three times have we had concurrence with the committee report, and then it was without debate.
So having examined all of the changes and made remarks on a few of them I just want to add that I think the acceptance of the proposal will benefit us all. It has shown the spirit of cooperation that can exist in this House, and I hope that during the year of trial it will all work out, and that the pitfalls which will undoubtedly be discovered will not be too great.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I will of necessity be brief. I want to thank the Conservative Party for the generosity which they have shown this evening. It is that spirit of co-operation that I know will keep the House operating on an even keel.
I was going to say that I found the debate this evening in keeping with the deliberations of the committee. I thought that the suggestions that were put forward on all sides were suggestions that, even in some cases critical, were intended to improve the report and improve the operations of the House of Commons and intended to support this new venture that we have all agreed to undertake.
Why did we undertake it? Because it became apparent that the Members of the House of Commons were either unable or unwilling to operate within the existing rules. It was a general opinion that the existing rules did not accommodate the new House of Commons in the sense of the new dynamics of the House of Commons, the new problems that had to be solved, the new methods that had to be found and the new initiatives that had to be taken.
The rules that we have offered can work. The question is, will they work? The rules that we had could have worked. They did not work.
November 29, 1982

This interim report of the committee will work provided that the Members of the House believe that it should work, believe that it is important that the House of Commons not only be able to act appropriately but that it be seen to be acting appropriately, which is equally important. Not only should we understand that what we are doing is correct, within the general structure and rules of the House, but the public should be able to understand how we are operating so they do not think that the House of Commons is in fact a circus. I believe that what we have before us is the first step, and in the course of the next few months we will see a number of reports which will further encourage the development of the Members' participation, and in so doing it will make the House of Commons much more relevant, and as we make it more relevant, the people of Canada will benefit substantially from it.

subtopic: GARRISON DIVERSION-REPORTED APPROVAL OF PROJECT BY UNITED STATES. (B) INQUIRY WHETHER STEPS TAKEN TO DETER ACTION IN U.S. CONGRESS
GARRISON DIVERSION-REPORTED APPROVAL OF PROJECT BY UNITED STATES. (B) INQUIRY WHETHER STEPS TAKEN TO DETER ACTION IN U.S. CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in light of the latest statements made in Grand Forks last week by Robert Wefald, the Attorney General for North Dakota, I find it imperative to stand this evening and call upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) to make an immediate appeal to Washington to curtail any further construction of the Garrison Diversion Project. Mr. Wefald, it appears, intends to totally disregard the affirmation of the International Joint Commission that the project would result in violation of the 1909 Boundary Waters Treaty between Canada and the United States.
The Attorney General for North Dakota is resolved to have the construction of the Garrison Water Diversion Project completed, despite opposition by the Canadian Government and the International Joint Commission, if the United States Government determines the project is in its best interests. Mr. Wefald is under the impression the potential contaminating effect of pumping water from the Missouri River across the continental divide into the Red River watershed "was blown all out of proportion". Obviously, the threat to the environment, that is, Manitoba's waterways, and particularly the threat to Manitoba's fishing industry, is being treated with indifference. Evidently, Mr. Wefald has not been made aware of, or has not had the opportunity to properly assess the various environmental studies and evaluations which have been done on the effects of water flowing north into Canadian waters.
All the evidence compiled by the scientists involved in the sutdy of this proposed project points to the disastrous effect it would have on Manitoba's agricultural and fishing industries as a result of flooding agricultural areas and disturbing the ecology in Manitoba's waterways. In light of the Attorney General's statements, it is quite apparent that the Manitoba New Democratic Party's office in Washington is having no effect at all in relaying our fears and concerns in regard to the Garrison project.
I call upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs to make clarification of the Attorney General's statements. As the NDP lobbying team seems to be inconsequential in blocking the continuation of the project, I repeat my call upon the federal Government, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs in particular, to launch a new and stronger protest to the Governor of North Dakota and to the appropriate people in Washington concerning the Garrison project.

November 29, 1982
Adjournment Debate
When we read statements such as those of the Attorney General of North Dakota, it is easily discernible that the endeavours of the NDP Office which was specifically set up to defend Manitoba's interests have been to little avail. Only 34 of the 435 members of the House of Representatives support the Canadian stand on the project. What have the lobbyists been doing all this time? The NDP does not appear to be particularly involved with, or have a commitment to establish the Canadian position on the Garrison project. If the NDP concerns were real, it would not allow the ruling of the International Joint Commission to be ignored. Representation should be made without delay to the proper officials in Washington to investigate the present state of affairs on the Garrison project, and to obtain verification of the intent of the United States on this issue.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean Lapierre (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: GARRISON DIVERSION-REPORTED APPROVAL OF PROJECT BY UNITED STATES. (B) INQUIRY WHETHER STEPS TAKEN TO DETER ACTION IN U.S. CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the Hon. Member I would like to point out that the long-standing Canadian position on the construction of the Garrison Diversion Unit remains that Manitoba waters and fisheries can only be adequately protected from serious damage or degradation resulting from the operation of the project if the Diversion Unit is modified in such a way that it does not result in water transfers from the Missouri River Basin into the waters of the Hudson Bay Basin flowing into Canada.
The U.S. administration is fully cognizant of this position which has been conveyed to them on numerous occasions in recent years. The U.S. Government has assured the Canadian Government that it will honour its obligations to Canada under the Boundary Waters Treaty not to pollute Canadian waters. The U.S. Government has also accepted the International Joint Commission Report on the Garrison Diversion Unit which recommended that the operations of the project which could affect waters flowing into Canada not be built at this time.
As Members may know, the U.S. administration has proposed the appropriation of $4 million for the Garrison project in fiscal year 1983-84. Although this amount is quite small in comparison to the $1.1 billion price tag of the entire project, Canadian authorities believe that the Garrison Diversion Unit should be re-designed before more money is spent on a project that will, as now designed, permit foreign biota to enter Canadian waters. Federal and Manitoba Ministers, as well as senior governmental officials in Ottawa, have stated this view very clearly to the U.S. administration.
In addition, Canadian officials have ensured that Members of the U.S. Congress are fully aware of Canadian views on this appropriation. Indeed, Members of Parliament and Senators have spoken directly to many Members of Congress earlier this year, reminding them of the significant Canadian interest at stake in this appropriation. All of these efforts, including those
by anti-Garrison groups in Manitoba, have ensured that Canadian views on the Project have been heard loud and clear on Capital Hill In Washington.
Regardless of the outcome of the appropriation vote, Canadian authorities will continue to insist that measures be taken by U.S. authorities to ensure that Manitoba waters and fisheries be protected from any injurious effects of the Garrison project. The Canadian side has a solid case on the Garrison issue and the Canadian Government will continue to strongly defend the interests of Canada and Manitoba in this project. We are counting very much on the support of the Hon. Member.

CONVENTION CENTRES-FINANCIAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO DEVELOPMENT OF RIDEAU CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening I would like to explain the circumstances of a recent event in my riding which attracted considerable attention and was widely reported in the press. I am, of course, referring to a decision by Eaton's to change the name of the Rideau Centre to Rideau Eaton Centre. As we all know, this decision was fiercely challenged by a number of local groups and by the population in general. On November 26, last Friday, Viking Rideau and Eaton's announced that they had decided to reverse their decision, and that the project would continue to be called the Rideau Centre or Centre Rideau. This evening, Mr. Speaker, I would like to give a short overview of this question to explain why local reaction to the change was negative. First of all, however, I must publicly congratulate Viking Rideau and the T. Eaton Company who demonstrated that a corporate citizen can be a good listener and a good citizen. Companies and corporations have a social role to play, and one can certainly say that the T. Eaton Company has taken this role seriously. I should therefore like to congratulate them once again for their attitude in this matter. My thanks are also directed to Messrs. David Howard and J. J. Barnicke, who are partners with Eaton's in the company that is developing the Rideau Centre.
Now for a look at the facts. First of all, we should remember that the Rideau Centre project is a joint enterprise which for over ten years has involved the public sector, represented by the Federal Government, the Department of Public Works, the National Capital Commission, the City of Ottawa and the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton, while the Government of Ontario was also involved in the Convention Centre. On the private sector side, there was Viking-Rideau, Westin Hotels, The Bay, Ogilvy's, Caplan and a number of other merchants. Since the project was initiated, co-operation among the various parties has always been excellent.
November 29, 1982

It was therefore a surprise for everyone when we learned in the press last November 10 that the T. Eaton Company wanted to change the name of the Rideau Centre to Eaton Rideau Centre. This unilateral decision made without any consultation was justified according to the company since Eaton holds 40 per cent of the shares in the Viking Rideau Company, which owns the Centre, and this makes it the major shareholder. Eaton believed that its name would add to the business potential of the Rideau Centre. The press was quick in spreading the news. This elicited an immediate reaction. For my part, I telephoned Mr. Eaton, the mayor of Ottawa, Mrs. Dewar, and the Chairman of the National Capital Commission, Mr. Drury. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) was also involved, as was the MP for Ottawa East, Mr. Albert Roy. On November 16, I also presented a motion under Standing Order 43 in the House about this matter.
There are many reasons to oppose the change in name. First, the Rideau sector project involves much more than the Eaton store. In fact, it concerns the whole centretown area of Ottawa, including Rideau Street, the Byward Market, Sandy Hill, Lower Town, and so on. At the time of its inception, the project had a rather wide-ranging objective, namely to upgrade the centre-town of Ottawa where the activities and infrastructures had been on the decline for many years. The Rideau Centre Project would bring new life to the area. However, the Eaton store alone will not bring about these changes. Other stores and many shops will open in the Rideau Centre, as well as hotels, restaurants and other businesses which will also be involved in the commercial upgrading of this sector. Therefore, while Eaton is a major business partner, it is not alone.
Another important factor is probably our cultural heritage. In the National Capital Region, the name "Rideau" designates part of our history. We have only to think about the Rideau River, the Rideau Canal, Rideau Hall, Rideau Street, and so on. Rideau is synonymous with Ottawa.

subtopic: CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-EVASION OF DUTIES BY AMWAY CORPORATION. (B) REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF POSSIBLE SETTLEMENT
CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-EVASION OF DUTIES BY AMWAY CORPORATION. (B) REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF POSSIBLE SETTLEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the corporate personification of the "American Way" is on trial both criminally and civilly today in Canada. On Wednesday, November 17 last, I asked the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) for an assurance that one of the largest direct sales companies in the world, namely Amway Corporation with sales last year of over $1.5 billion, would not be allowed to make a quiet deal with the Canadian Government to settle four outstanding civil actions. That same day the Company
was charged by the Ontario Attorney General with defrauding the Canadian Government under the Criminal Code. The trial date was set for tomorrow, Tuesday, November 30, 1982. I understand the Company announced today that it did not intend to put in an appearance. This, of course, shows complete contempt for the Canadian judicial process.
Amway, short for the American Way, was in fact found guilty in 1979 by the American Federal Trade Commission of fixing retail and wholesale prices and misrepresenting the profitability of Amway distributorships. The Company is headed by a Mr. Jay Van Andel and Richard M. DeVos, two of the five largest contributors to Ronald Reagan's campaign and the owners of the Mutual Broadcasting System, which is the largest radio network in the United States. Mr. Van Andel was from 1979 to 1980 the Chairman of the United States Chamber of Commerce and a good friend of Gerry Ford. Mr. DeVos, until he was fired in August, was the National Chairman of the Republican Fund Raising Committee. Amway as well, I might add, is an important supporter of the National Right to Work, Legal Defence and Education Foundation. We have here a classic case of free enterprise getting greedy and going sour in an attempt to maximize its profits by duping Canadian officials.
Revenue Canada has alleged that for 1977 to 1980 alone, Amway dramatically undervalued its goods entering Canada. Apparently this procedure has been going on since 1965. The claim for this three-year period alone is some $148 million covering over 1,700 separate entries. I understand that a Canadian customs broker blew the whistle on Amway.
Some of the internal documents which I have seen constitute a searing indictment of the attempts by Amway Corporation, this American corporate giant and its largest subsidiary, Amway of Canada, to avoid the payment of literally millions and millions of dollars in Canadian customs duties and thereby defraud Canadian taxpayers of millions of dollars. I intend to quote in the short time available to me some of the salient extracts from those documents.
Dummy invoices apparently were prepared, and in one of the documents dated December, 1975, an internal company document, it is stated:
No actual transactions take place between Amway and the contract warehouses.
The invoices are never sent to the contract warehouses and never paid by them. The contract warehouses are not aware of the existence of the invoices.
It continues:
A sharp auditor could request proof that the invoices were actually paid by the contract warehouses. No such proof exists.
In a document from the Vice-president, dated 1978, it is stated that the prices at which Amway of Canada has purchased products from Amway Corporation have been supported for purposes of Canadian customs duties as being proper by means of false representations, both oral and written. Canadian counsel has confirmed that the conduct practised constitutes fraud.
November 29, 1982

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-EVASION OF DUTIES BY AMWAY CORPORATION. (B) REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF POSSIBLE SETTLEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to reassure this House that at no time have information exchanges between the Department and Amway taken the form of negotiations. I repeat, there have been no negotiations and no secret deals and there will be none.
However, there have been exchanges of information between the parties to ensure that all facts relevant to the issues are
Adjournment Debate
clear to all. This has taken place within the normal adjudication process of the Department carried out under the Customs Act, Sections 160 to 168.
When goods become subject to seizure or forefeiture, the Department forwards to the interested party a formal notice of seizure pursuant to Section 161 of the Customs Act. This gives the party involved the opportunity to present, within 30 days of the date the notice has been issued, any information pertinent to the case. After the expiration of that period, the Department has the authority to consider and weigh the circumstances of the case and render a decision under Section 163 of the Customs Act.
In 1979, acting upon information that there might be irregularities by Amway regarding its imports to Canada, the Department immediately initiated an investigation. Shortly thereafter the RCMP was brought into the investigation.
In 1980, the Department, you will recall, informed Amway of its conclusions and filed four claims in the Federal Court, totalling $148 million. This represents the duty paid value of the goods imported. That is the value for duty of the goods imported, determined in accordance with the provisions of Canadian customs law, plus duty and taxes on this value.
In the case of Amway, the adjudication process was suspended on the advice of the Department of Justice, pending the decision of the Attorney General of Ontario concerning the question of laying criminal charges against the company, the Department having first protected its position by filing these claims.
Criminal charges were laid by the Attorney General of Ontario on November 12, 1982, and the Department is consulting with its lawyers to determine the appropriate course of action to follow respecting completion of the normal adjudication process.
It has been and is the normal practice of the Department to recognize that where a value for duty, albeit too low a value, has been declared at the time of entry and duty and taxes have been paid on that value, the final decision will take this amount into account by allowing it as a deduction from the gross amount claimed. Thus, Amway was advised that the final decision would probably be in the order of $105 million. Again following normal practice, the Department has continued to maintain its four claims in the Federal Court for the gross amount of $148 million.
The question has been asked whether we would ask for interest on the sum due to the Crown by Amway. Let me remind you that the Customs Act does provide for a penalty significantly greater than the duties and taxes not paid. It has not been the practice to seek interest except in some cases where the Department has agreed to deferred payment arrangements.
As you know the Department does not normally disclose information concerning penalties paid under the Customs Act. However, in this case the Department intends to disclose this

November 29, 1982
Adjournment Debate
information, in the public interest, in a way which will not prejudice the interest of any of the parties involved.
